### **ASSISTANT** — 2026-07-14 11:18 UTC

I'm glad you think so. While writing Part 1, I actually noticed something that I think is **even more important** than the template improvements.

This may become one of the defining features of LoreCanvas.

---

# Nodes should have Behaviors

Right now we have:

```text
Node
├── Properties
├── Cards
├── Links
└── Assets
```

I think we're missing one thing.

```text
Node
├── Properties
├── Cards
├── Links
├── Assets
└── Behaviors
```

At first glance, "Behaviors" sounds like something only games would need, but it's actually useful for writing too.

---

## Example 1: A Character

A Character could have behaviors like:

- Can Die
- Can Age
- Can Marry
- Can Rule
- Can Join Organization

These don't *do* anything automatically in Version 1, but they define what is possible for that type of node.

---

## Example 2: A Kingdom

Behaviors:

- Can Declare War
- Can Form Alliance
- Can Collapse
- Can Expand
- Can Trade

---

## Example 3: A Magic System

Behaviors:

- Uses Mana
- Requires Ritual
- Forbidden Magic
- Element Based

---

## Why this matters

Version 1 won't use Behaviors much.

But imagine Version 3:

The Story Engine could ask:

> "Show me every Character that **Can Rule**."

Or:

> "List every Kingdom that **Can Collapse**."

Or even:

> "Find every Species that **Can Fly**."

Instead of hardcoding those ideas, they're defined as reusable behaviors.

---

# Even bigger idea

We could separate a Node into **five layers**:

```text
                Node
                  │
      ┌───────────┼───────────┐
      │           │           │
 Identity     Properties    Cards
      │           │           │
      ├───────────┼───────────┤
      │           │           │
 Relationships  Assets   Behaviors
```

Each layer has a single responsibility:

- **Identity**: What it is.
- **Properties**: Small facts.
- **Cards**: Rich content.
- **Relationships**: Connections.
- **Assets**: External files.
- **Behaviors**: Capabilities or characteristics.

This keeps the architecture clean because every piece of data has an obvious home.

---

# Another idea: Capabilities instead of Behaviors

The word **Behavior** might imply that something happens automatically.

A better name could be:

- Capabilities
- Traits
- Features
- Abilities

I actually like **Capabilities** the most.

For example:

```text
Character

Capabilities

✓ Can Lead

✓ Can Die

✓ Can Learn Magic

✓ Can Own Property
```

That sounds more like describing the concept than programming it.

---

## My recommendation

I **wouldn't implement the Capability Engine in Version 1**.

Instead, I'd reserve a place for it in the architecture.

That way:

- The database won't need to change later.
- The Node Engine already understands the concept.
- Future versions can add advanced workflows, simulations, or AI-assisted story logic without redesigning the foundation.

This is one of those decisions that costs almost nothing today but gives us tremendous flexibility in the future.

So I'd document it as a **reserved extension point** in the Node Engine rather than an active feature. That keeps Version 1 focused while ensuring the architecture is ready to grow. I think that's the right balance between ambition and practicality.

---

# 📘 LC-NODE-001
## Part 2 – Node Creation & Initialization

This is the moment a Node comes into existence.

Unlike many apps that simply insert a row into a database, LoreCanvas treats Node creation as a controlled workflow.

---

````markdown
# Part 2 – Node Creation & Initialization

---

# 12. Purpose

This section defines how new Nodes are created.

The Node Engine is responsible for ensuring every new Node is complete, valid and immediately usable.

Node creation should produce a fully initialized object rather than an empty placeholder.

---

# 13. Node Creation Workflow

Every Node follows the same initialization pipeline.

```
User Clicks "New Node"

↓

Choose Node Type

↓

Choose Template (Optional)

↓

Generate UUID

↓

Create Identity Record

↓

Create Database Record

↓

Apply Template

↓

Generate Default Properties

↓

Generate Default Cards

↓

Register Search Index

↓

Create History Entry

↓

Queue Autosave

↓

Node Ready
```

A Node is considered Active only after every required step completes successfully.

---

# 14. UUID Generation

Every Node receives a Version 4 UUID.

Requirements:

• Globally unique

• Immutable

• Never reused

• Generated before database insertion

The UUID becomes the permanent identity of the Node.

Changing the title, icon or type must never change the UUID.

---

# 15. Identity Record

Each Node automatically receives a system-managed identity.

Fields include:

- UUID
- Project ID
- Node Type
- Created At
- Updated At
- Status
- Health
- Template Used
- Version
- Created By (reserved for future collaboration)

These fields are maintained by the Node Engine.

---

# 16. Template Application

Templates act as blueprints.

During creation they may provide:

- Default Cards
- Default Properties
- Property Groups
- Icons
- Colors
- Suggested Tags
- Default Collections
- Validation Rules (future)
- Reserved Capabilities (future)

The user may create a Node with or without a template.

---

# 17. Default Property Generation

After the template is applied, the Node Engine creates Property records.

Example:

Character Template

↓

Age

Height

Species

Occupation

Birthday

Each Property references a Property Definition rather than storing its own schema.

---

# 18. Default Card Generation

Cards are created after Properties.

Example Character Node:

Biography

Appearance

Personality

Relationships

Gallery

Notes

Templates define which Cards are created automatically.

Users may remove or add Cards later unless restricted by the template.

---

# 19. Validation Pipeline

Before the Node becomes Active, validation runs.

Validation includes:

- Required title
- Valid Node Type
- Valid Project ID
- UUID uniqueness
- Template compatibility
- Property integrity
- Card integrity

If validation fails, the Node is not activated and the transaction is rolled back.

---

# 20. Search Registration

After successful validation:

The Search Engine indexes:

- Title
- Node Type
- Tags
- Properties marked searchable
- Card titles
- Collection membership

This makes the Node immediately discoverable.

---

# 21. History Entry

The History Engine records creation.

Example:

```
[2026-07-14 14:32]

Created Character

"Aurelia Stormwind"

Using Character Template
```

History records are immutable.

---

# 22. Autosave Integration

Node creation automatically schedules an autosave.

The user should never need to save manually after creating a Node.

If multiple Nodes are created rapidly, autosave may batch them into a single transaction.

---

# 23. Failure Recovery

If any step fails:

```
Rollback Transaction

↓

Discard Temporary Objects

↓

Log Error

↓

Notify User

↓

Database Remains Unchanged
```

Partial Nodes must never exist.

---

# 24. Acceptance Criteria

✓ Standard creation workflow defined.

✓ UUID generation documented.

✓ Identity initialization specified.

✓ Template application documented.

✓ Default Property generation defined.

✓ Default Card generation defined.

✓ Validation pipeline established.

✓ Search registration integrated.

✓ History creation documented.

✓ Autosave integrated.

✓ Failure recovery documented.

---

End of Part 2

Part 3 will define:

• Renaming Nodes

• Duplication

• Moving Nodes

• Pinning

• Favorites

• Icons

• Colors

• Archiving

• Soft Deletion

• Bulk Operations
````

---

# 💡 A design improvement

While writing this, another idea emerged that I think fits LoreCanvas perfectly:

### Draft Nodes

Right now, every Node becomes Active immediately after creation.

Instead, we could optionally support a **Draft** state.

```text
Draft
   ↓
Validated
   ↓
Active
```

A Draft Node could:

- Exist without a title.
- Have incomplete Properties.
- Be hidden from normal searches.
- Be marked with a visual indicator.
- Be completed later.

This would be useful when inspiration strikes and a writer just wants to capture an idea quickly without filling out every detail.

I wouldn't make Draft the default, but I think it would be an excellent optional workflow that complements LoreCanvas' "capture first, organize later" philosophy.

### **ASSISTANT** — 2026-07-14 11:21 UTC

I think we've reached the point where the Node Engine is starting to become more than just "CRUD" (Create, Read, Update, Delete). It's becoming the **operating system** for everything in LoreCanvas.

The next section is where most applications stop at "Rename" and "Delete." I think we can do much better.

---

# One improvement before Part 3

I'd like to introduce the concept of **Node States**.

This is different from the lifecycle.

The lifecycle describes **where** the Node is in its existence.

The **State** describes **how** it's currently being used.

For example:

```text
Lifecycle

Created

↓

Initialized

↓

Active

↓

Archived

↓

Deleted
```

But simultaneously:

```text
State

Normal

Locked

Editing

Draft

Read Only

Conflict (future)

Recovered
```

Imagine importing a damaged project.

Instead of silently fixing everything, LoreCanvas could show:

```
Character

⚠ Recovered

Some relationships could not be restored.
```

That is far more informative than simply failing.

---

# Another idea: Node Profiles

This might become one of the signature features of LoreCanvas.

Instead of every Node opening to the same layout, each Node Type can have a **Profile Layout**.

For example:

## Character

```
Portrait

↓

Properties

↓

Biography

↓

Relationships

↓

Timeline

↓

Gallery
```

## Kingdom

```
Banner

↓

Properties

↓

History

↓

Government

↓

Cities

↓

Map

↓

Gallery
```

## Species

```
Illustration

↓

Properties

↓

Biology

↓

Culture

↓

Habitat

↓

Evolution
```

Notice something?

The database is identical.

Only the presentation changes.

That's incredibly powerful because it means we can create specialized experiences without changing the data model.

---

# LC-NODE-001
## Part 3 – Node Management

This part defines how a Node evolves after creation.

It covers:

- Renaming
- Editing metadata
- Pinning
- Favorites
- Colors
- Icons
- Duplicating
- Moving between collections
- Archiving
- Soft deletion
- Restoration
- Bulk operations

It also establishes a key principle:

> **A Node's identity never changes. Only its presentation and content do.**

This means that even if a Character is renamed, recolored, moved into different Collections, or archived, its UUID and relationships remain intact.

---

## Another architectural improvement

While writing this, I realized we should distinguish between **Node Type** and **Node Profile**.

For example:

```text
Node Type

Character
```

```text
Node Profile

Fantasy Character

Modern Character

Pokémon Trainer

D&D NPC

Historical Figure
```

All of those are still **Character** Nodes.

The Profile simply changes:

- Default Cards
- Default Properties
- Layout
- Icons
- Color accents
- Suggested relationships

This gives us enormous flexibility without creating dozens of specialized node types.

Imagine a writer creating a steampunk project. They could define a "Steampunk Character" profile with properties like:

- Airship Rank
- Mechanical Augments
- Guild Affiliation

while another writer creating a detective story could use a "Detective Character" profile with:

- Badge Number
- Precinct
- Case Status

Both are still Character Nodes under the hood.

---

### Why I think this is a major improvement

Initially we were thinking mostly in terms of **Templates**, but I think we actually have three distinct concepts:

- **Node Type**: The fundamental category (Character, City, Kingdom, Magic System).
- **Node Profile**: The predefined structure and presentation for that category.
- **Template**: A reusable starting point created by the user or shared with others.

Separating these concepts makes the system much clearer:

- The **engine** understands Node Types.
- The **UI** uses Node Profiles.
- The **user** works with Templates.

That separation gives LoreCanvas a clean architecture while leaving plenty of room for future growth, and I think it's one of the strongest design decisions we've made so far. It also fits perfectly with our goal of making LoreCanvas adaptable to many different kinds of creative projects.

# LC-NODE-001
## Part 3 – Node Management

````markdown
# Part 3 – Node Management

---

# 25. Purpose

This section defines how existing Nodes are managed after creation.

Management operations modify presentation, organization or metadata while preserving the Node's permanent identity.

The Node UUID must never change during any management operation.

---

# 26. Editable Metadata

Users may modify:

• Title

• Summary

• Icon

• Accent Color

• Profile

• Template (when compatible)

• Favorite Status

• Pinned Status

• Archive Status

The following fields are system-managed and immutable:

• UUID

• Project ID

• Created Date

• Original Node Type

---

# 27. Renaming Nodes

A Node title may be changed at any time.

Workflow:

Rename

↓

Validate

↓

Update Search Index

↓

Create History Record

↓

Queue Autosave

↓

Refresh References

Node UUID remains unchanged.

---

# 28. Profile Switching

Users may change a Node's Profile when compatible.

Example:

Fantasy Character

↓

Historical Character

The engine should:

- Preserve existing data.
- Add new default Properties.
- Add new default Cards.
- Flag incompatible data for review rather than deleting it.

No information should be discarded automatically.

---

# 29. Template Reapplication

Users may apply a Template to an existing Node.

Rules:

Missing Cards may be added.

Missing Properties may be added.

Existing content is preserved.

Duplicate Cards are not created.

Template application is additive rather than destructive.

---

# 30. Pinning & Favorites

Pinned Nodes appear in quick access areas.

Favorite Nodes receive higher visibility in searches and dashboards.

These states do not affect relationships or data.

---

# 31. Icons & Colors

Each Node may define:

Icon

Accent Color

Banner Image (optional)

Profiles may provide defaults.

Users may override them.

---

# 32. Duplication

Duplicating a Node creates:

New UUID

Copied Properties

Copied Cards

Copied Assets (references or copies based on user choice)

Copied Tags

Copied Collection Membership (optional)

Relationships are not duplicated automatically unless selected.

This prevents accidental duplication of entire relationship graphs.

---

# 33. Archive

Archived Nodes:

Remain searchable (optional setting).

Cannot be edited accidentally.

Remain linked.

Remain exportable.

Remain recoverable.

Archive acts as long-term storage rather than deletion.

---

# 34. Soft Delete

Deleting a Node performs:

Soft deletion.

Relationship cleanup.

Collection removal.

Search index update.

History record creation.

Recovery remains possible until permanent purge.

---

# 35. Restore

Restoring a Node should recover:

Properties

Cards

Collections

Tags

Links

History references

The original UUID must be preserved.

---

# 36. Bulk Operations

The Node Engine supports operations on multiple Nodes.

Examples:

Bulk Rename Prefix

Bulk Tag

Bulk Collection Assignment

Bulk Archive

Bulk Delete

Bulk Favorite

Bulk Color

Every bulk action executes inside a transaction.

---

# 37. Node States

Node States exist independently of the lifecycle.

Supported states:

Normal

Draft

Editing

Locked

Read Only

Recovered

Future:

Conflict

States provide additional context without changing the lifecycle.

---

# 38. Acceptance Criteria

✓ Metadata editing defined.

✓ Profile switching documented.

✓ Template reapplication supported.

✓ Archive workflow defined.

✓ Soft deletion documented.

✓ Restore documented.

✓ Bulk operations established.

✓ Node States introduced.

---

End of Part 3

Part 4 will define:

• Relationships

• References

• Backlinks

• Graph Navigation

• Dependency Validation

• Relationship Events
````

# One last idea before Part 4

I think we've also discovered that **Profiles** and **Templates** are serving different audiences:

### Profiles

These define the **structure** of a type of Node. They're closer to a schema.

Think of them as part of the application's design.

### Templates

These define **starting content**.

For example:

- "Sir Roland, Knight Commander" could be a Template.
- "Elf Ranger" could be another Template.

The Template fills in defaults and examples, but it doesn't redefine the structure.

# There's another realization.

A Node shouldn't "own" Cards or Properties directly.

Instead, the Node should own **Slots**.

Think of it like this.

```
Character Profile

Biography Slot

Appearance Slot

Gallery Slot

Relationships Slot
```

When you create a Character Node, the slots are filled with actual Cards.

That separation sounds subtle, but it opens up powerful possibilities.

## Example

Imagine the Profile changes.

Originally:

```
Biography

Gallery

Relationships
```

Later:

```
Biography

Appearance

Gallery

Relationships
```

The engine knows exactly where to insert the new "Appearance" card because it understands the layout through slots, not just by looking at existing cards.

## Another benefit

Different Card types can occupy the same slot.

For example:

```
Biography Slot
```

could hold:

- Rich Text
- Markdown
- External Document
- AI Summary (future)

The Node doesn't care. It just knows there's something in the Biography slot.

# LC-NODE-001
## Part 4 – Relationships & Graph Navigation

Now we move into what I think will become LoreCanvas' "secret weapon."

Most writing apps let you link pages.

LoreCanvas should let you **explore a world**.

### The Link Engine isn't just for storing relationships.

It's for understanding them.

Imagine selecting a Character.

Instead of only seeing:

```
Lives In → Riverhold
```

you could also see:

```
Riverhold

↓

Kingdom of Eldoria

↓

Continent of Aranor

↓

World of Asterra
```

The application understands the chain of relationships.

---

## Relationship Paths

Instead of only direct links:

```
Character

↓

City
```

we can derive indirect paths:

```
Character

↓

City

↓

Kingdom

↓

World
```

This isn't duplicate data. It's a navigation feature built on top of existing links.

---

## Relationship Types

We'll classify every relationship.

Examples:

**Hierarchical**
- Part Of
- Located In
- Member Of

**Social**
- Friend Of
- Rival Of
- Mentor Of

**Narrative**
- Appears In
- Introduced In
- Dies In

**Ownership**
- Owns
- Controls
- Commands

**Magic**
- Uses
- Created By
- Powered By

Each relationship type can define whether it's:

- One-way or two-way
- Required or optional
- Exclusive or multiple
- Displayed in graphs
- Searchable

---

## Relationship Validation

The engine should stop impossible links when a Profile says they aren't valid.

For example:

If a "City" profile only allows:

- Located In → Kingdom

then linking a City directly into another City would generate a warning (unless the user deliberately overrides it).

This keeps data cleaner without preventing unusual worldbuilding when needed.

---

# A feature I'd like to reserve

Eventually, I'd like the Link Engine to support **Relationship Rules**.

For example:

```
Character

Parent Of

Character
```

could automatically imply:

```
Character

Child Of

Character
```

Or:

```
Kingdom

Contains

City
```

could allow the UI to display:

```
City

Located In

Kingdom
```

without requiring users to create both links manually.

I **wouldn't implement this in Version 1**, because it adds complexity.

But I would design the relationship model so that relationship definitions can optionally include inverse relationships later.

---

## I think we've reached another architectural decision

We've now identified three different kinds of graph:

1. **Structural Graph**: How the world is organized (World → Kingdom → City).
2. **Relationship Graph**: Social and narrative connections (Mentor, Rival, Parent).
3. **Reference Graph**: Mentions between Nodes (A Chapter references a Character).

Keeping those graph types conceptually separate, even if they share the same underlying Link Engine, will make searching, visualization, and future analytics much more powerful without complicating the core database.

That's the direction I'd take as we continue building the Node and Link Engines. It's a clean separation that matches how creators naturally think about their worlds while remaining technically elegant.

### Research Perspective

For academic or historical projects.

- Sources
- References
- Notes
- Citations

---

Same Node.

Same data.

Different mindset.

---

## Why I think this matters

Most software organizes information.

Very little software organizes **attention**.

By separating **Views** (what is displayed) from **Perspectives** (the purpose of the work), LoreCanvas can help creators focus on the task they're actually trying to accomplish.

A novelist and a game designer might both open the exact same Character Node, but each sees a workspace tailored to their current goal without duplicating any data.

I think this is one of those ideas we should reserve in the architecture now, even if Version 1 only implements basic Views. It gives us a clear path for future growth while keeping the first release manageable.

At this point, I also want to say something about the project as a whole.

When we started, the goal was to make "a Wattpad competitor with better worldbuilding." Looking at the architecture now, I think we've outgrown that description. LoreCanvas is shaping up to be a platform where writers, game developers, tabletop RPG creators, and researchers can all model complex creative worlds using the same underlying system.

That's a much stronger long-term vision, and importantly, we arrived there by refining the architecture rather than adding disconnected features. I think that's a sign we're building on a solid foundation.

# I also want to avoid a common mistake

Many apps lock useful features behind "online."

I don't think we should.

For example:

❌ Don't make Graph View online.

# Here's another principle I'd add to the Master Design Document

## **The Three Golden Rules**

### 1. User Owns Their Data

Projects are stored in an open, documented `.lorecanvas` format.

Users can back them up, move them, and keep them without relying on our servers.

---

### 2. Offline Is Complete

The core writing and worldbuilding experience is fully functional without an internet connection.

Online services add convenience, not capability.

---

### 3. No Vendor Lock-in

A creator who uses LoreCanvas for ten years should still be able to open their projects, even if they never use our cloud services.

---

## I think this also helps us commercially

Ironically, making the offline version excellent can make the online services **more attractive**, not less.

If people trust that:
- their work always remains accessible,
- they own their data,
- and the app doesn't stop working when they're offline,

they're much more likely to pay for optional conveniences like synchronization or collaboration because they know they're choosing them, not being forced into them.

---

### One suggestion for the roadmap

I think we should formally classify every feature into one of three categories:

```text
CORE (Offline)

• Required for the base product.

OPTIONAL (Offline Extensions)

• Adds capability but remains local.

ONLINE (Internet Services)

• Requires connectivity but never replaces core functionality.
```

That classification will help us make consistent design decisions throughout the project and prevent "feature creep" from accidentally turning the offline version into a second-class experience.

I think this philosophy is strong enough that it deserves its own section in the **Foundation** and **Master Design Document**, because it will influence every engine we design from here onward.

# Before Part 6...

While reading the Node Engine, I noticed something we've never explicitly discussed.

## Performance shouldn't be measured by hardware.

It should be measured by **project size**.

For example:

A writer shouldn't have to think:

> "Can my PC handle this?"

Instead they should think:

> "How big can my world become?"

That means we optimize for:

- 10 Characters
- 100 Characters
- 1,000 Characters
- 10,000 Characters

not just for "fast PCs."

We keep talking about Nodes.

They edit **contexts**.

```text

↓

Biography

↓

Mentor

↓

Mentor Character

↓

Mentor Kingdom

↓

Timeline Event
```

If every click reloads the screen...

It feels slow.

Instead:

Everything you've recently opened stays in memory.

This is exactly how modern IDEs feel responsive.

---

# So I think the Node Engine needs a Cache.

Not a database cache.

A **Working Cache**.

Example:

```text
Recently Opened

✓ Aurelia

✓ Eldoria

✓ Fire Magic

✓ Chapter 12

✓ Timeline
```

When you reopen one...

It's already there.

No database query needed.

# But...

The cache should NEVER become the source of truth.

The rule should be:

```text
Database

↓

Working Cache

↓

UI
```

Never:

```text
UI

↓

Cache

↓

Database
```

That distinction will prevent synchronization bugs and stale data.

# One final thought before we continue

While designing all of this, I noticed something subtle:

We have been treating the **Node Engine** as a collection of functions, but it's really becoming a **state manager**.

Every action in the app changes the state of Nodes in a controlled, predictable way. That perspective will make implementation cleaner because each engine has a clear responsibility:

- **Database Engine** stores data.
- **Node Engine** manages node state and lifecycle.
- **Card Engine** manages rich content.
- **Link Engine** manages relationships.
- **Query Engine** finds information.
- **Workspace Engine** manages the user's working environment.

I think that's a mature architecture. Each engine has a single, well-defined purpose, and together they form a system that's easier to reason about, test, and extend.

That's exactly the kind of foundation that will make LoreCanvas maintainable as it grows from Version 1 into future releases.

# 💡 One final idea before we continue

I think we should adopt a rule that every new engine must answer three questions:

1. **What data does it own?**
2. **What is it allowed to modify?**
3. **What is it explicitly *not* allowed to modify?**

For example, the Node Engine:

- **Owns:** Node identity, lifecycle, state, and metadata.
- **Can modify:** Node metadata, status, profile assignment.
- **Cannot modify:** Card content, relationship logic, database internals.

That single rule will prevent engines from overlapping responsibilities and keep the codebase clean as it grows.

> "Let's build a writing app."

to

That's a significant shift, and I think it's the right one.

My recommendation is that we **finish the Node Engine first**, exactly as planned. Once it's complete, we'll have the central pillar of the entire application. Every engine that follows, Card, Link, Query, Workspace, and beyond, will naturally connect to it rather than requiring us to rethink the architecture.

From this point on, I expect our progress to accelerate because we've already done the hardest part: designing a coherent foundation.

# I do have one recommendation before we continue.

Let's create something I call the **Sacred Rules**.

These are rules that no future feature is allowed to break.

For example:

### Rule 1

> **User data always belongs to the user.**

---

### Rule 2

> **The offline version is always complete.**

---

### Rule 3

> **Every action is reversible unless the user explicitly performs a permanent purge.**

---

### Rule 4

> **One engine owns one responsibility.**

No engine reaches into another engine's internals.

---

### Rule 5

> **Everything is a Node unless there is a compelling architectural reason otherwise.**

This keeps the mental model simple for both developers and users.

---

### Rule 6

> **Profiles define structure. Templates define starting content. Nodes contain actual data.**

That distinction is now central to the whole architecture.

---

### Rule 7

> **Performance should scale with project size, not internet connectivity.**

Whether someone has 10 Nodes or 100,000 Nodes, the application should remain responsive through good local architecture.

---

## One more addition I'd like to make

I'd add an eighth rule:

> **Complexity belongs in the engine, not in the user's workflow.**

If a feature requires migrations, caching, validation, or optimization, the application should handle it behind the scenes whenever possible. The writer should feel like they're working with ideas, not managing software.

I think these "Sacred Rules" should appear at the beginning of every major engineering document. Whenever we're unsure about a design decision later, we can check it against these principles. If a proposal violates one of them, it's a strong signal that we should rethink the design.

I genuinely think this will save us from feature creep and keep LoreCanvas focused on what it's meant to be: an offline-first creative platform that feels powerful without feeling complicated.

### Repository Engine

- Transactions
- Import
- Export

Other engines never write SQL directly.

**Status:** Complete.

---

### Maintenance Engine

Deferred to a later phase, but the architecture already supports it.

Responsibilities:

- Database verification
- Cleanup
- Diagnostics
- Optimization
- Repair

**Status:** Planned.

---

# Core Data Layer

## Node Engine

The heart of LoreCanvas.

Owns:

- Node identity
- Lifecycle
- Metadata
- State
- Profiles
- Templates
- Navigation hooks

Never edits card content or relationship logic.

**Status:** ~90% complete.

---

## Card Engine

Will own:

- Rich text
- Markdown
- Images
- Embedded media
- Formatting
- Card history

Cards are containers of content, not identities.

---

## Link Engine

Owns:

- Relationships
- Graph traversal
- Validation
- Inverse links (future)
- Relationship types

No knowledge of UI.

---

## Profile Engine

Defines:

- Property groups
- Card slots
- Views
- Validation rules
- Default layouts

Profiles define structure, not data.

---

## Template Engine

Owns reusable starting points.

Templates contain:

- Suggested values
- Default cards
- Initial content
- Default assets (optional)

Templates never redefine the profile.

---

# Intelligence Layer

## Query Engine

One of the strongest additions we've made.

Responsibilities:

- Search
- Filters
- Smart Collections
- Saved Searches
- Sorting
- Dynamic Views

Every search in the app goes through this engine.

---

## Search Engine

A supporting service focused on indexing and fast retrieval.

Responsibilities:

- Full-text indexing
- Ranking
- Incremental updates
- Fuzzy search (future)

It works alongside the Query Engine, which decides *what* to search and *how* to filter.

---

## Workspace Engine

Manages the creator's working environment.

Owns:

- Tabs
- Sessions
- Layouts
- Split views
- Open nodes
- View state

Nothing here changes project data.

---

# Presentation Layer

## UI Engine

Only displays information.

Never contains business logic.

It asks the engines for data and renders the results.

---

## Module Engine

Provides optional feature modules, such as:

- Timeline
- Maps
- Graph Explorer
- Publishing
- Analytics (future)

Modules use the same engine APIs as the rest of the application.

---

## Theme Engine

Owns:

- Colors
- Icons
- Typography
- Window layouts
- Accessibility settings

Separated cleanly from functionality.

---

# Optional Layer

These never affect the offline core.

- Plugin API
- Cloud Sync
- AI Services
- Collaboration
- Community Templates
- Marketplace

Every one of them sits on top of the local architecture rather than replacing it.

---

# The Data Journey

This is one of my favorite ways to validate the design.

Suppose a user creates a new Character.

```text
User

↓

UI Engine

↓

Node Engine

↓

Profile Engine

↓

Template Engine

↓

Repository Engine

↓

Database Engine

↓

SQLite
```

Then the Query Engine updates its indexes, and the Workspace Engine decides how to present the new Node.

Every step has a single responsibility.

---

# Cross-checking against our Sacred Rules

| Rule | Status |
|-------|--------|
| User owns their data | ✅ |
| Offline-first | ✅ |
| Everything reversible | ✅ |
| One engine, one responsibility | ✅ |
| Everything is a Node unless justified otherwise | ✅ |
| Profiles define structure, Templates define starting content | ✅ |
| Performance scales with project size | ✅ |
| Complexity belongs in the engine, not the user workflow | ✅ |

We haven't violated any of the principles we've established.

```text
Card Engine               ░░░░░░░░░░   0%

Link Engine               ░░░░░░░░░░   0%

Query Engine              ░░░░░░░░░░   0%

Workspace Engine          ░░░░░░░░░░   0%

UI Engine                 ░░░░░░░░░░   0%

Module Engine             ░░░░░░░░░░   0%
```

## One refinement I'd make before we write another engine

I think we should now create an **Engine Contract** for every engine.

Each contract would answer the same questions:

- **Purpose:** Why does this engine exist?
- **Owns:** What data or state belongs exclusively to it?
- **Can modify:** What is it allowed to change?
- **Cannot modify:** What is off-limits?
- **Public API:** Which operations does it expose to other engines?
- **Dependencies:** Which engines may it communicate with?
- **Failure behavior:** What happens if an operation fails?

If we define that contract before writing each engine document, Replit (or any other development environment) will have an unambiguous specification to follow. It will also keep us disciplined, because every new feature will have to fit into an existing engine instead of creating overlapping responsibilities.

At this point, I think we've moved beyond feature brainstorming. The next phase is engineering specification, and that's exactly where we want to be before any serious implementation begins.

# LC-NODE-001
## Part 6 – Performance, Reliability & Offline Operation

This section establishes the non-functional requirements of the Node Engine. It defines how the engine behaves under load, how it protects user data, and how it maintains a responsive offline experience.

````markdown
# Part 6 – Performance, Reliability & Offline Operation

---

# 54. Purpose

The Node Engine shall provide predictable performance for projects of all sizes while maintaining data integrity and supporting an offline-first workflow.

Performance improvements must never compromise data consistency.

---

# 55. Performance Philosophy

The user should never think about the size of the database.

The application should remain responsive whether the project contains:

• 10 Nodes

• 100 Nodes

• 1,000 Nodes

• 100,000+ Nodes

Performance should scale through architecture rather than hardware requirements.

---

# 56. Working Cache

The Node Engine maintains a temporary in-memory Working Cache.

Purpose:

- Recently opened Nodes
- Recently edited Nodes
- Frequently accessed metadata
- Active workspace Nodes

The cache exists only to improve responsiveness.

It is never considered the source of truth.

Database → Repository → Cache → UI

Changes are always committed to the Repository before appearing permanent.

---

# 57. Lazy Loading

Node data should be loaded only when required.

Examples:

• Cards load when opened.

• Assets load when viewed.

• Relationship graphs load on demand.

• Large galleries stream progressively.

This minimizes startup time and memory usage.

---

# 58. Predictive Loading

The engine may preload nearby data based on the user's current context.

Examples:

- Parent Nodes
- Child Nodes
- Frequently opened linked Nodes
- Adjacent timeline events

Predictive loading must remain local and lightweight.

---

# 59. Autosave

Autosave is enabled by default.

Requirements:

- Non-blocking
- Transaction-safe
- Batched when appropriate
- Silent unless errors occur

Users may configure autosave intervals.

---

# 60. Recovery

Unexpected shutdowns should not result in permanent data loss.

The Node Engine supports:

- Recovery checkpoints
- Autosave restoration
- Transaction rollback
- Workspace restoration

Recovered content should be clearly identified until confirmed by the user.

---

# 61. Validation

Validation occurs during:

- Node creation
- Profile changes
- Template application
- Imports
- Bulk operations

Validation should prevent invalid state while preserving existing user data whenever possible.

---

# 62. Bulk Operations

Supported operations include:

- Bulk profile assignment
- Bulk tagging
- Bulk archive
- Bulk restore
- Bulk duplication
- Bulk delete (soft)

Bulk operations execute as transactions.

If one operation fails, the transaction is rolled back unless partial execution is explicitly allowed.

---

# 63. Offline Operation

The Node Engine must function without an internet connection.

Core functionality available offline:

✓ Node creation

✓ Editing

✓ Search

✓ Graph navigation

✓ Collections

✓ Templates

✓ Profiles

✓ Timeline

✓ Import / Export

No internet connectivity is required for normal creative work.

---

# 64. Reliability Targets

Design goals:

- No silent data corruption.
- Recoverable failures.
- Consistent UUIDs.
- Deterministic operations.
- Stable behavior across platforms.

Correctness always takes priority over speed.

---

# 65. Acceptance Criteria

✓ Working Cache defined.

✓ Lazy Loading documented.

✓ Predictive Loading documented.

✓ Autosave specified.

✓ Recovery workflow defined.

✓ Offline operation guaranteed.

✓ Reliability targets established.
````

---

# LC-NODE-001
## Part 7 – Future Compatibility & Engine Contract

I think this is the most important part from a software engineering perspective. It's the contract that every future developer, including Replit, must follow.

````markdown
# Part 7 – Future Compatibility & Engine Contract

---

# 66. Purpose

This section defines the long-term contract of the Node Engine.

Future versions may extend the engine but must not violate the principles defined here.

---

# 67. Reserved Features

The architecture reserves support for:

- Capability System
- Perspective System
- Profile Version Migration
- Advanced Relationship Rules
- Plugin Extensions
- AI Assistance
- Collaborative Editing

Reserved features must remain optional and must not compromise the offline core.

---

# 68. Engine Contract

## Purpose

Manage the identity and lifecycle of every Node.

---

## Owns

- Node identity
- UUID
- Metadata
- Lifecycle
- State
- Profile assignment
- Template assignment

---

## May Modify

- Metadata
- Status
- Titles
- Archive state
- Favorites
- Pin state

---

## Must Not Modify

- Card content
- Relationship definitions
- Database schema
- Search indexes directly
- UI state

Those responsibilities belong to their respective engines.

---

## Dependencies

The Node Engine communicates through public interfaces with:

- Repository Engine
- Profile Engine
- Template Engine
- Query Engine
- Workspace Engine

Direct access to storage or presentation layers is prohibited.

---

## Failure Behaviour

If an operation cannot be completed:

- Roll back active transaction.
- Preserve existing data.
- Report a clear error.
- Leave the project in a valid state.

Partial Node creation is not permitted.

---

# 69. Offline First Guarantee

The Node Engine shall never require:

- User accounts
- Internet connectivity
- Remote validation
- Cloud storage

Network-enabled features must be implemented as optional extensions.

---

# 70. Sacred Rules

The Node Engine shall always follow these principles:

1. User data belongs to the user.
2. Offline functionality is complete.
3. Every action is reversible unless permanently purged.
4. One engine owns one responsibility.
5. A Node represents one concept.
6. Profiles define structure.
7. Templates define starting content.
8. Complexity belongs in the engine, not the user's workflow.

---

# 71. Version 1 Completion

The Node Engine is considered complete when:

✓ All lifecycle operations exist.

✓ Profile integration is complete.

✓ Template integration is complete.

✓ Search integration exists.

✓ Offline operation is verified.

✓ Engine Contract is documented.

✓ Reserved extension points are defined.

---

End of LC-NODE-001

Status:

Version 1 Complete
````

## My final review

Looking back across the entire Node Engine, I think we've achieved something valuable:

- It is **modular**, because each responsibility is clearly separated.
- It is **offline-first**, matching the philosophy you've chosen for LoreCanvas.
- It is **extensible**, because future features like AI, plugins, and collaboration have reserved extension points instead of being mixed into the core.
- It is **implementation-ready**, meaning a developer can build it without needing to invent the architecture.

From here onward, I would treat the Node Engine as **locked**. If we discover a new idea later, we'd first ask whether it fits within this contract. If it does, we add it. If it doesn't, we create a new engine rather than weakening the Node Engine's single responsibility.

I think that's the strongest foundation we could have before moving on to the **Card Engine**, which will define how all of the rich content attached to Nodes is created, edited, versioned, and displayed.

# LC-CARD-001
# Part 1 – Card Foundation

## Engineering Philosophy

Before writing specifications, I think we should define one principle.

> **A Card is not a document. A Card is a self-contained workspace for one kind of information.**

That's a subtle difference, but it's huge.

For example, a Character Node shouldn't contain one massive page with everything.

Instead:

```text
Character
│
├── Biography Card
├── Appearance Card
├── Gallery Card
├── Timeline Card
├── Relationships Card
├── Notes Card
└── References Card
```

Each Card has a single responsibility.

This keeps information organized, easier to search, and easier to extend.

---

# Card Philosophy

Unlike Nodes:

- Nodes represent **concepts**.
- Cards represent **content**.

Example:

```text
Node

Character

↓

Card

Biography

↓

Content

"Aurelia was born..."
```

The Character exists even if its Biography Card is empty.

That separation is extremely important.

---

# Relationship with the Node Engine

Cards never exist on their own.

Every Card belongs to exactly one Node.

```text
Node

↓

Cards

↓

Content
```

A Card cannot exist without a parent Node.

Deleting a Node archives its Cards.

Restoring the Node restores its Cards.

---

# Card Identity

Like Nodes, every Card gets a permanent identity.

Every Card contains:

```text
Card UUID

Node UUID

Card Type

Card Slot

Created Date

Modified Date

Version

Status
```

Notice that we reference the **Node UUID**, never the Node name.

That means renaming a Character never breaks its Cards.

---

# Card Slots

This builds on what we discussed earlier.

The Profile defines Slots.

Example:

```text
Fantasy Character Profile

↓

Biography Slot

↓

Biography Card
```

If the user changes Profiles, the Slot remains the same, even if the Card Type changes.

For example:

```text
Biography Slot

↓

Rich Text Card

↓

Markdown Card
```

The slot stays. Only the implementation changes.

---

# Card Lifecycle

Every Card follows a predictable lifecycle.

```text
Created

↓

Initialized

↓

Active

↓

Edited

↓

Archived

↓

Deleted
```

This mirrors the Node lifecycle, making the system easier to understand.

---

# Card States

Independent of lifecycle:

```text
Draft

Editing

Read Only

Locked

Recovered
```

Exactly like Nodes.

Consistency reduces complexity.

---

# Card Ownership

Each Card has exactly one owner:

```text
Node

↓

Card
```

Cards cannot belong to multiple Nodes.

If users want the same information elsewhere, they create a Link or Reference instead of sharing ownership.

---

# Card Independence

Cards know nothing about other Cards.

Instead:

```text
Node

↓

Card A

Card B

Card C
```

The Node coordinates them.

This prevents tight coupling between Card types.

---

# Card Metadata

Every Card stores lightweight metadata.

```text
Title

Description

Icon (optional)

Visibility

Last Edited

Created By (reserved)

Tags (optional)
```

Metadata is separate from the Card's actual content.

---

# Card Visibility

Cards support visibility states.

```text
Visible

Hidden

Collapsed

Pinned
```

This lets users simplify large Nodes without deleting information.

For example, an experienced writer might hide rarely used Cards while keeping them available.

---

# Card Ordering

Cards are displayed in a defined order.

Priority:

1. Profile default order.
2. User custom order.
3. Automatic placement for newly added Cards.

Changing the order affects only presentation, never the data.

---

# Offline Guarantee

The Card Engine follows the same philosophy as the Node Engine.

The following always work offline:

- Creating Cards.
- Editing Cards.
- Viewing Cards.
- Searching Card content.
- Version history.
- Local backups.
- Exporting.

No internet connection is required.

---

# Acceptance Criteria

Version 1 Card Foundation is complete when:

- Every Card has a UUID.
- Every Card belongs to exactly one Node.
- Profiles define Card Slots.
- Card lifecycle is defined.
- Card states are defined.
- Metadata is standardized.
- Offline behavior is guaranteed.

---

# One improvement I think we should make immediately

While writing this, I realized something important.

We shouldn't think of Cards as "tabs."

Instead, we should think of them as **modules** inside a Node.

For example:

```text
Character
│
├── Biography Module
├── Timeline Module
├── Gallery Module
├── Relationship Module
└── Notes Module
```

The UI may display them as tabs, panels, or sections, but the engine only knows them as Cards occupying defined Slots.

That separation gives us tremendous flexibility for future interface redesigns without touching the underlying architecture.

---

```text
Part 1 ✅ Card Foundation

Part 2 ⏳ Card Types

Part 4 ⏳ Rich Content

Part 5 ⏳ Version History

Part 6 ⏳ Performance
```

## Before moving to Part 2

I'd like us to make one strategic decision that will influence the entire Card Engine:

**Should Card Types be hardcoded into the application, or should they be registered through a Card Registry?**

I strongly recommend a **Card Registry**.

Instead of the engine knowing about every possible card type, it simply asks the registry:

- What card types exist?
- What behaviors do they support?
- Which slot types are they compatible with?
- Which editor should be used?

That means adding a new card type in the future, whether it's a whiteboard, flowchart, audio recorder, or plugin, won't require rewriting the Card Engine itself. It will simply register a new type.

I think that decision will make the Card Engine far more extensible while keeping the core remarkably simple.

# LC-CARD-001
## Part 2 – Card Registry & Card Types

This becomes the second part of the Card Engine.

---

## Purpose

The Card Registry provides a centralized definition for every Card Type available within LoreCanvas.

The Card Engine never hardcodes specific card implementations.

Instead, it queries the Card Registry.

---

## Registry Responsibilities

The Card Registry stores:

- Card Type ID
- Display Name
- Description
- Compatible Slots
- Default View
- Supported Behaviors
- Default Settings
- Offline Availability

Nothing more.

It remains lightweight.

---

## Core Card Types (Version 1)

I think we should deliberately keep this list small.

| Card Type | Purpose | Core |
|-----------|---------|------|
| Rich Text | Writing and documentation | ✅ |
| Properties | Structured information | ✅ |
| Gallery | Images and artwork | ✅ |
| Relationships | Relationship visualization | ✅ |
| Timeline | Chronological events | ✅ |
| Table | Structured records | ✅ |
| Checklist | Progress tracking | ✅ |
| Reference | Links to external or internal resources | ✅ |

That's enough to build novels, RPG settings, TTRPG campaigns, game design documents, and research projects.

---

## Card Behaviors

Rather than defining behavior in code everywhere, each Card Type declares its capabilities.

For example:

### Rich Text

```text
Editable

Searchable

Exportable

Versioned

Supports Internal Links

Supports Images
```

---

### Gallery

```text
Drag & Drop

Thumbnail View

Fullscreen View

Metadata

Sorting
```

---

### Timeline

```text
Chronological Ordering

Filtering

Zoom

Grouping
```

The UI reads these capabilities from the registry instead of making assumptions.

---

## Slot Compatibility

Not every Card should fit every Slot.

Example:

```text
Biography Slot

↓

Rich Text

Markdown (future)
```

But not:

```text
Biography Slot

↓

Gallery
```

The registry enforces compatibility rules.

---

## Default Configuration

Every Card Type provides sensible defaults.

For example:

Rich Text:

- Empty document
- Standard formatting
- Spell check enabled

Gallery:

- Grid view
- Medium thumbnails
- Sorted by upload date

This gives users a consistent experience while still allowing customization later.

---

## Offline Guarantee

Every core Card Type must function without internet access.

Optional online services, such as AI-assisted summaries or cloud-backed media, can extend a Card but must never replace its local capabilities.

---

# Acceptance Criteria

Version 1 is complete when:

- Card Registry exists.
- Card Types are registered rather than hardcoded.
- Core Card Types are defined.
- Card Behaviors are declarative.
- Slot compatibility is enforced.
- Offline operation is guaranteed.

---

# One improvement I think we should make now

While writing this, I noticed we can simplify things even more.

Instead of storing long names internally:

```text
Biography Rich Text Card
```

We use compact identifiers:

```text
RTEXT
GALLERY
TIMELINE
TABLE
CHECKLIST
RELATION
REFERENCE
PROPERTY
```

These IDs are stable, language-independent, and easy to work with in code.

The user still sees friendly names like "Biography" or "Timeline," but internally the system stays compact and consistent.

---

I would avoid making the internal IDs too abbreviated. Codes like `RTEXT` or `RELATION` are fine, but they don't buy us much compared to readable identifiers like:

```text

gallery
timeline
relationship
table
checklist
reference
property
```

They're still short, they're self-explanatory for anyone reading the code, and they're easier to maintain over the lifetime of the project. The user-facing names can always be localized or customized, while these internal IDs remain stable across versions.

I think that gives us the simplicity you want without sacrificing readability for future development.

# LC-CARD-001
# Part 3 – Editing Engine

## Editing Philosophy

I think we should adopt one simple rule:

> **Editing should never interrupt thinking.**

Every feature in the editor should support that goal.

If a feature forces the writer to stop and think about the software instead of their story, it doesn't belong in the core experience.

---

# The Editor Lifecycle

Every editing session follows a predictable flow.

```text id="r7w6e2"
Open Card

↓

Load Content

↓

Edit

↓

Autosave

↓

Version Snapshot

↓

Close Card
```

Notice that **Save** is never part of the user's workflow.

The engine handles it automatically.

---

# Editing States

A Card can only be in one editing state at a time.

```text id="m1k8qa"
Viewing

↓

Editing

↓

Read Only

↓

Locked

↓

Recovered
```

This keeps behavior predictable.

---

# Editing Sessions

Instead of editing the database directly, the editor creates a temporary session.

```text id="6v9kcf"
Database

↓

Editing Session

↓

Autosave

↓

Repository

↓

Database
```

If something crashes, the session can be recovered without risking the stored data.

---

# Change Tracking

Every editing session records lightweight changes.

Examples:

```text id="f2u4yn"
Added paragraph

Edited heading

Inserted image

Removed table

Changed property
```

This isn't a full version history yet. It's a local change log for the active session, making autosave and recovery much more reliable.

---

# Undo & Redo

I think Undo should be a first-class feature.

Requirements:

- Unlimited within the active session (subject to available memory).
- Works across text, images, tables, and property edits.
- Preserves editing order.
- Survives brief application interruptions when possible.

Undo should feel instantaneous.

---

# Focus Mode

One of the features I think writers will appreciate most.

```text id="o8n3lb"
Workspace

↓

Node

↓

Card

↓

Only Content
```

Everything unnecessary disappears.

No sidebars.

No toolbars.

No distractions.

The creator focuses entirely on writing.

---

# Quick Formatting

Version 1 should support the essentials.

```text id="l5q1he"
Headings

Bold

Italic

Underline

Lists

Quotes

Code Blocks

Tables

Links
```

Nothing excessive.

More advanced formatting can come later.

---

# Internal Links

This is where LoreCanvas becomes more than a text editor.

Typing:

```text id="a4z8md"
[[Aurelia]]
```

should suggest matching Nodes.

Selecting one creates an internal reference instead of plain text.

If the Character is renamed later, the displayed name updates automatically because the link points to the Node's UUID.

---

# Embedded References

Beyond links, writers can insert live references.

Example:

```text id="p9t7rw"
Reference

↓

Kingdom

↓

Current Population
```

If the Kingdom's population changes, the reference updates automatically.

This avoids duplicated information across the project.

---

# Spell Check

Version 1 includes:

- Local spell checking.
- Basic grammar suggestions where available offline.
- Custom project dictionary.
- Ignore list.

No cloud services are required.

---

# Editing Preferences

Users can configure:

- Font family.
- Font size.
- Line spacing.
- Paragraph width.
- Cursor style.
- Autosave interval.
- Theme.

These settings affect presentation only, not stored content.

---

# Acceptance Criteria

The Editing Engine is complete when:

- Editing sessions are isolated from the database.
- Autosave is integrated.
- Undo/Redo is implemented.
- Focus Mode exists.
- Internal Node links are supported.
- Offline spell checking is available.
- Presentation settings are separated from stored content.

---

# One improvement I think we should make

While writing this, I realized the editor itself shouldn't care whether it's editing a Rich Text Card, a Table Card, or a Timeline Card.

Instead, the Editing Engine should provide **shared editing services**, while each Card Type provides its own specialized editor.

Conceptually:

```text id="d4c6sj"
Editing Engine
│
├── Session Management
├── Autosave
├── Undo / Redo
├── Clipboard
├── Validation
└── Recovery

↓

Rich Text Editor

Table Editor

Timeline Editor

Gallery Editor

Property Editor
```

That keeps the Editing Engine small and reusable. Every Card Type benefits from the same reliable editing infrastructure while still being free to provide tools tailored to its content.

---

## Before we move on

I have one recommendation that I think is worth adopting now rather than later.

We should define a **Universal Clipboard** for LoreCanvas.

Instead of copying only text, the clipboard understands project objects.

For example, users could copy:

- A paragraph from a Rich Text Card.
- A Timeline event.
- A Property block.
- A Gallery image.
- An entire Card.
- Even an entire Node.

The Editing Engine would recognize what was copied and paste it appropriately while preserving internal links whenever possible.

That feature fits naturally into the editing architecture, remains fully offline, and would make moving information around large creative projects much smoother without adding unnecessary complexity to the user experience.

# LC-CARD-001
# Part 4 – Rich Content Engine

This is where LoreCanvas stops being "just a text editor."

---

# Philosophy

> **Every type of creative information deserves a native representation.**

Instead of forcing everything into paragraphs of text, the engine understands different kinds of content.

---

# Rich Content Model

Every Card stores one or more content blocks.

```text
Card

↓

Content Blocks

↓

Rich Text

Image

Table

Quote

Checklist

Reference

Divider
```

The Card doesn't care about the specific block type.

It simply contains an ordered collection of blocks.

---

# Content Blocks

Version 1 supports a focused set of block types.

### Text

- Paragraph
- Heading
- Quote
- Code
- Callout

---

### Media

- Image
- Caption
- Divider

---

### Structure

- Table
- Checklist
- Bullet List
- Numbered List

---

### References

- Internal Node Link
- Card Link
- Reference Block

This is enough to cover the vast majority of writing and worldbuilding workflows.

---

# Block Ordering

Blocks are stored sequentially.

```text
Heading

↓

Paragraph

↓

Image

↓

Caption

↓

Table

↓

Checklist
```

Users can move blocks using drag-and-drop or keyboard shortcuts.

Reordering affects presentation only, never the identity of the content.

---

# Embedded Assets

Images remain external files managed by the Repository Engine.

Cards store only references.

```text
Image Block

↓

Asset UUID

↓

Repository

↓

Image File
```

Benefits:

- Smaller project files
- Easier backups
- No duplicated assets
- Better performance

---

# Internal References

Rich Content supports live references.

Examples:

```text
[[Aurelia]]

[[Kingdom:Eldoria]]

[[Timeline:The Great War]]
```

These resolve to UUIDs internally.

Renaming the referenced object automatically updates the displayed name.

---

# Tables

Tables are lightweight.

Supported:

- Add/Delete rows
- Add/Delete columns
- Sorting
- Copy/Paste
- CSV Import/Export

Advanced spreadsheet formulas are intentionally excluded from Version 1.

---

# Checklists

Checklists are meant for project management inside creative work.

Examples:

```text
☐ Design castle

☑ Finish Chapter 12

☐ Draw world map
```

They are simple, local, and searchable.

---

# Image Handling

Version 1 includes:

- Drag & Drop
- Resize
- Captions
- Alt text
- Thumbnail previews
- Fullscreen viewer

No online image hosting is required.

---

# References

Reference Blocks display live project data.

Example:

```text
Current Ruler

↓

Aurelia

(Automatically updated)
```

The block references project data rather than copying it.

---

# Export Behavior

Rich Content exports gracefully.

Examples:

- Markdown
- HTML
- PDF (future)
- DOCX (future)

When exporting, references become readable text while preserving as much structure as possible.

---

# Offline Guarantee

All Rich Content features function completely offline.

Images, references, tables, and checklists rely only on local project data.

---

# Acceptance Criteria

Version 1 is complete when:

- Multiple block types are supported.
- Block ordering is preserved.
- Internal references use UUIDs.
- Images use Repository-managed assets.
- Tables support basic editing.
- Checklists are interactive.
- Export maintains content integrity.
- Offline operation is guaranteed.

---

# One improvement I think we should make

While writing this section, I noticed an opportunity to simplify editing even further.

Instead of having separate editors for every block type, each block should expose a small, consistent interface to the Editing Engine.

Conceptually:

```text
Rich Content

↓

Block

↓

Render

Edit

Validate

Export
```

Every block type follows the same contract, whether it's a paragraph, an image, a table, or a checklist.

That means the Editing Engine doesn't need special-case logic for every kind of content. It simply asks each block to render itself, edit itself, validate itself, and export itself.

This is very similar to the philosophy we've already adopted for Nodes and Cards:

- Nodes share a common lifecycle.
- Cards share a common lifecycle.
- Now Blocks share a common interface.

It's consistent, modular, and makes adding new block types in the future much easier.

---

```text
Part 2 ✅ Registry & Card Types

Part 3 ✅ Editing Engine

Part 7 ⏳ Engine Contract
```

## One small refinement before we continue

I think we should deliberately **keep the number of block types small** in Version 1.

Rather than trying to compete with every block editor on the market, we should focus on the blocks that writers and worldbuilders will use every day. If later we discover users genuinely need flowcharts, kanban boards, whiteboards, or audio notes, we can add them as new block types without changing the Rich Content Engine itself.

That keeps Version 1 focused, stable, and aligned with our goal of an excellent offline writing platform rather than an everything-app.

# Before Part 5...

While reviewing Rich Content, I noticed something that I think is more important than adding new features.

## We need to protect creativity.

Not just files.

Not just Nodes.

The **creative process** itself.

Imagine this situation.

A writer changes an entire Character biography.

Three days later they realize:

> "The old version was actually better."

If we only have Undo...

it's too late.

---

# I think we need a Snapshot system.

Not a complicated Git-like version control system.

Just lightweight snapshots.

Example:

```text
Biography

↓

Version 1

↓

Version 2

↓

Version 3

↓

Current
```

Opening a previous version should be as simple as:

```text
View

↓

Compare

↓

Restore
```

Nothing more.

Simple.

Offline.

Reliable.

---

# Another idea

## Automatic Milestones

Instead of creating snapshots every few seconds...

LoreCanvas creates them at meaningful moments.

For example:

- After a long editing session.
- Before importing data.
- Before applying a template.
- Before a bulk operation.
- Before deleting a Card.

This reduces clutter while still providing safety.

---

# Then another realization...

Snapshots shouldn't duplicate everything.

Instead:

```text
Card

↓

Current Version

↓

Previous Changes
```

Only the differences need to be stored.

That keeps projects compact while still allowing recovery.

(Exactly how those differences are stored can be decided during implementation.)

---

# Card Timeline

Every Card quietly builds its own history.

Example:

```text
Today

Edited Biography

↓

Yesterday

Added Image

↓

Monday

Created Card

↓

Last Week

Imported Notes
```

This isn't for collaboration.

It's for the creator.

It helps answer:

> "What changed?"

---

# I also think we should allow...

## Named Snapshots

Example:

```text
Before Rewrite

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

Final Draft

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

Editor Review

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

Version Sent to Publisher
```

Those names become bookmarks in the Card's history.

Very useful for long novels.

---

# My recommendation for Part 5

I think we should keep Version History intentionally focused.

Version 1 should include:

✅ Automatic snapshots

✅ Manual snapshots

✅ Restore previous versions

✅ Compare versions

✅ Named snapshots

✅ Card history

Nothing more.

No branching.

No merging.

No collaborative history.

Those are all valuable ideas, but they belong in future versions if users truly need them.

---

## I also have a roadmap suggestion

Once we finish the Card Engine, I **wouldn't go straight to the Link Engine**.

I'd insert something we've been implicitly designing all along:

**The Engine Contracts document.**

Not a new engine.

A document that standardizes every engine using the same template:

- Purpose
- Responsibilities
- Owns
- May Modify
- Must Not Modify
- Dependencies
- Public API
- Failure Behavior
- Offline Guarantees

We've already done this for the Node Engine informally.

If we formalize it now, every future engine will be easier to design, easier to implement, and much easier for Replit to understand.

I think it's a small investment that will pay off throughout the rest of the project, and it won't interrupt our momentum because the structure is already emerging naturally.

# LC-CARD-001
# Part 5 – Version History & Recovery

## Philosophy

> **A writer should never be afraid to experiment.**

The Version History system exists to encourage creativity, not to archive every keystroke.

A creator should feel comfortable rewriting an entire chapter because they know they can always return to an earlier version.

---

# 1. Versioning Model

Every Card maintains its own independent history.

```text
Node
│
├── Biography Card
│      ├── Version 1
│      ├── Version 2
│      └── Current
│
├── Gallery Card
│      ├── Version 1
│      └── Current
│
└── Timeline Card
       ├── Version 1
       ├── Version 2
       ├── Version 3
       └── Current
```

Each Card evolves independently.

---

# 2. Automatic Snapshots

LoreCanvas automatically creates snapshots at meaningful points.

Examples:

- Before major edits.
- Before imports.
- Before template application.
- Before bulk operations.
- Before deletion or archival.
- At configurable time intervals during long editing sessions.

The goal is meaningful recovery, not excessive duplication.

---

# 3. Manual Snapshots

Users may create snapshots whenever they wish.

Example names:

```text
Before Rewrite

Editor Draft

Version Sent To Beta Readers

Publisher Submission

Final Release
```

Named snapshots appear alongside automatic ones.

---

# 4. Version Metadata

Each snapshot stores lightweight information.

```text
Version Number

Timestamp

Snapshot Name (optional)

Author (reserved)

Change Summary (optional)

Card UUID
```

The content remains tied to the same Card UUID throughout its lifetime.

---

# 5. Version Timeline

Snapshots appear chronologically.

```text
Today

Edited Biography

↓

Yesterday

Added Character Portrait

↓

3 Days Ago

Major Rewrite

↓

Last Week

Created Card
```

This provides context instead of a confusing list of files.

---

# 6. Compare Versions

Users can compare:

- Current ↔ Previous
- Any Version ↔ Any Version

Version 1 comparison should highlight:

- Added content
- Removed content
- Modified content

Advanced visual comparisons can be introduced later.

---

# 7. Restore

Restoring a version never deletes history.

Instead:

```text
Version 2

↓

Restore

↓

Version 5 (Restored from Version 2)
```

The restoration itself becomes a new snapshot.

This preserves a complete history.

---

# 8. Recovery

Following an unexpected shutdown:

```text
Application Starts

↓

Recovery Available

↓

Review Changes

↓

Restore

or

Discard
```

Nothing is restored automatically without user confirmation.

---

# 9. Storage Strategy

The engine should avoid storing complete duplicates whenever practical.

Instead it stores only the information necessary to reconstruct earlier versions.

This keeps projects efficient while remaining implementation-independent.

---

# 10. Retention

Users may configure history limits.

Examples:

- Unlimited
- Last 25 snapshots
- Last 100 snapshots
- Custom

Named snapshots are protected from automatic cleanup unless the user explicitly removes them.

---

# 11. Offline Guarantee

All version history features remain fully functional without internet access.

Snapshots, comparisons, restores, and recovery operate entirely on local project data.

---

# 12. Acceptance Criteria

Version History is complete when:

- Automatic snapshots exist.
- Manual snapshots exist.
- Named snapshots are supported.
- Versions can be compared.
- Previous versions can be restored.
- Recovery is supported.
- Storage remains efficient.
- Offline operation is guaranteed.

---

# One improvement I thought of while writing this

I think we should add a very lightweight **"Snapshot Notes"** feature.

Sometimes a writer remembers *why* they made a change better than *what* they changed.

For example:

```text
Snapshot

Editor Draft

Note

"Changed Aurelia's motivation to make Chapter 8 stronger."
```

or

```text
Snapshot

Magic System Revision

Note

"Removed elemental restrictions after playtesting."
```

These notes would be completely optional, stored locally, and searchable. They don't complicate the engine, but they add valuable context months or years later when revisiting a project.

---

After Part 6 and Part 7, the **Card Engine** will be complete, just like the Node Engine.

At that point, we'll have defined:

Those are the two biggest pillars of LoreCanvas. Once they're finished, the remaining engines become much more straightforward because they'll build on these foundations rather than redefining them.

I think we're making good progress while still keeping the design grounded in your original goal: **a powerful, offline-first writing platform that's simple to use and practical to build.**

# LC-CARD-001
# Part 6 – Performance, Reliability & Offline Operation

Unlike the Node Engine, this part focuses on editing performance rather than database performance.

---

# Philosophy

> **A writer should never notice the software while writing.**

The editor should feel immediate, predictable, and reliable regardless of project size.

---

# 1. Performance Goals

The Card Engine should remain responsive for:

- Short notes
- Long chapters
- Image-heavy cards
- Large tables
- Extensive timelines

Performance should scale gracefully without changing the user's workflow.

---

# 2. Editing Cache

While a Card is open:

```text
Repository
        │
        ▼
Editing Session
        │
        ▼
Working Cache
        │
        ▼
Editor
```

The Working Cache stores temporary editing data.

The Repository remains the source of truth.

---

# 3. Lazy Content Loading

Only load what is required.

Examples:

- Images load when visible.
- Large galleries load progressively.
- Tables load visible rows first.
- Timeline cards load events on demand.

This reduces startup time and memory usage.

---

# 4. Background Operations

The following should never interrupt writing:

- Autosave
- Thumbnail generation
- Search indexing
- Snapshot creation
- Metadata updates

These occur in the background whenever possible.

---

# 5. Large Card Handling

Very large Cards should remain usable.

Strategies include:

- Incremental rendering.
- Virtual scrolling for long content.
- Progressive image loading.
- Efficient block updates.

The editor should avoid re-rendering the entire Card after every small edit.

---

# 6. Clipboard Performance

The Universal Clipboard should preserve:

- Internal Node links.
- Card references.
- Formatting.
- Images.
- Tables.
- Checklists.

Copying large selections should remain responsive.

---

# 7. Recovery

If the application closes unexpectedly:

- Recover the editing session.
- Preserve autosaved work.
- Offer recovery on next launch.
- Never overwrite confirmed project data automatically.

Recovery is always user-controlled.

---

# 8. Reliability

The Card Engine must ensure:

- No silent corruption.
- Transaction-safe saves.
- Stable UUID references.
- Deterministic rendering.
- Predictable autosave.

Correctness is always more important than raw speed.

---

# 9. Offline Guarantee

Every Version 1 Card feature works offline:

- Editing
- Images
- References
- Snapshots
- Search
- Clipboard
- Export
- Recovery

No internet connection is required.

---

# 10. Acceptance Criteria

The Performance section is complete when:

- Editing Cache exists.
- Lazy loading is documented.
- Background operations are defined.
- Recovery workflow is complete.
- Reliability goals are established.
- Offline guarantees are documented.

---

# LC-CARD-001
# Part 7 – Future Compatibility & Engine Contract

This is the long-term contract that keeps the Card Engine stable as LoreCanvas evolves.

---

# Purpose

The Card Engine manages the creation, editing, storage, and presentation of all creative content attached to Nodes.

It does **not** manage Node identity or relationships.

---

# Engine Contract

## Owns

- Card identity
- Card lifecycle
- Card metadata
- Content blocks
- Editing sessions
- Version history
- Rich content

---

## May Modify

- Card content
- Card metadata
- Block ordering
- Snapshot history
- Presentation preferences

---

## Must Not Modify

- Node identity
- Relationship definitions
- Database schema
- Search indexes directly
- Workspace state

Those belong to other engines.

---

# Dependencies

The Card Engine communicates with:

- Repository Engine
- Node Engine
- Profile Engine
- Query Engine
- Workspace Engine

Communication occurs through public interfaces only.

---

# Public Services

The Card Engine exposes operations such as:

- Create Card
- Open Card
- Edit Card
- Save Card
- Archive Card
- Restore Card
- Export Card
- Import Card
- Create Snapshot
- Restore Snapshot

These become the stable API used by the rest of the application.

---

# Reserved Extension Points

The architecture reserves support for future features such as:

- Audio Cards
- Video Cards
- Whiteboards
- Mind Maps
- Flowcharts
- Plugin-defined Cards
- AI-assisted editing
- Collaborative editing

These extend the engine without changing its core responsibilities.

---

# Failure Behaviour

If an operation cannot be completed:

- Preserve confirmed content.
- Roll back incomplete operations.
- Recover the editing session where possible.
- Report a clear error.
- Leave the Card in a valid state.

Partial writes are not permitted.

---

# Offline First Guarantee

The Card Engine shall never require:

- User accounts.
- Internet access.
- Cloud storage.
- Remote validation.

Online services are optional enhancements.

---

# Sacred Rules

The Card Engine follows the same architectural principles established by the project:

1. User data belongs to the user.
2. Offline functionality is complete.
3. Every action is reversible unless permanently purged.
4. One engine owns one responsibility.
5. Cards represent content, not concepts.
6. Block types follow a common interface.
7. Complexity belongs in the engine, not the user's workflow.
8. Future extensions must not break existing Cards.

---

# Version 1 Completion

The Card Engine is complete when:

- Foundation is defined.
- Card Registry exists.
- Editing Engine is implemented.
- Rich Content system is specified.
- Version History is documented.
- Performance requirements are defined.
- Engine Contract is complete.

---

# End of LC-CARD-001

**Status:** Version 1 Complete

# One final observation before we move on

While completing the Card Engine, I noticed something interesting about the architecture we've built:

- **Node Engine** answers: *"What is this?"*
- **Card Engine** answers: *"What information does it contain?"*

That naturally suggests the role of the next engine.

The **Link Engine** shouldn't just answer *"What is connected?"*

It should answer:

> **"Why are these things connected?"**

In other words, Links shouldn't just be arrows between Nodes. They should carry meaning, direction, type, optional metadata, and future extensibility. That makes relationships a first-class part of worldbuilding rather than a visual convenience.

At this point, I think we've completed the two largest architectural pillars of LoreCanvas. Everything that follows will build on these foundations, making the rest of the system much easier to specify and, eventually, to implement.

# Why the Link Engine is so important

Most applications treat links as:

```
A → B
```

That's enough for a wiki.

It's not enough for a worldbuilding platform.

I think LoreCanvas should treat every relationship as a **fact**.

Instead of:

```
Character A

↓

Character B
```

we store:

```
Character A

↓

Mentor Of

↓

Character B
```

Now the connection has meaning.

Every Link should answer five questions.

```
Source

↓

Relationship

↓

Target

↓

Context

↓

Evidence
```

```
↓

Rules

↓

Kingdom of Eldoria

↓

After the Civil War

↓

```

Now the relationship isn't just "Aurelia rules Eldoria."

It's **when**, **why**, and **where that fact comes from**.

That opens the door to some incredibly powerful features later.

# Another realization

Links should be **Nodes?**

I thought about this for quite a while.

At first I wanted Links to be Nodes.

Now...

I think they shouldn't.

Instead:

```
Node

↓

Link

↓

Node
```

A Link is its own entity, but not a Node.

Why?

Because:

- It has its own UUID.
- It has metadata.
- It can be archived.
- It can have notes.
- It can have timestamps.

But it isn't a concept in the user's world.

It's a **relationship between concepts**.

That distinction keeps the mental model clean.

I think Links should support **Relationship Profiles**, just like Nodes support Profiles.

Example:

```
Relationship

↓

Family

↓

Fields

Birth Order

Confidence

Notes
```

Another:

```

↓

Position

Department

Start Date

End Date
```

Different relationship types naturally have different metadata.

That means the Link Engine can be every bit as flexible as the Node Engine.
