# LC-LINK-001
# Part 1 – Link Foundation

## Engineering Philosophy

> **A Link represents a meaningful relationship between two concepts.**

It is not merely a visual connector.

A Link stores meaning, context, and metadata while remaining independent of how it is displayed.

---

# What is a Link?

A Link always connects exactly two Nodes.

```text id="lv9ef8"
Source Node

↓

Relationship

↓

Target Node
```

Examples:

```text id="kn7j1u"
Aurelia

↓

Rules

↓

Kingdom of Eldoria
```

```text id="8w1obm"
Iron Sword

↓

Forged In

↓

Blackstone Forge
```

```text id="8q5k0q"
Dragon

↓

Lives In

↓

Northern Mountains
```

The Link carries the meaning, not just the connection.

---

# Link Identity

Every Link has its own permanent identity.

```text id="2ehm8w"
Link UUID

Source Node UUID

Target Node UUID

Relationship Type

Created Date

Modified Date

Status
```

Notice that the relationship references Node UUIDs rather than names.

Renaming either Node never breaks the Link.

---

# Link Lifecycle

Links follow the same lifecycle philosophy as Nodes and Cards.

```text id="w2jlv7"
Created

↓

Validated

↓

Active

↓

Modified

↓

Archived

↓

Deleted
```

Consistency across engines makes the application easier to understand.

---

# Link States

Independent of the lifecycle, a Link may be:

```text id="zvx0f3"
Active

Hidden

Archived

Recovered
```

These states control visibility and availability without changing the underlying relationship.

---

# Relationship Types

Every Link has one Relationship Type.

Examples:

```text id="zq5m4q"
Parent Of

Lives In

Rules

Member Of

Friend Of

Enemy Of

Owns

Created

Uses

Located In
```

The type gives the relationship its meaning.

---

# Direction

By default, Links are directional.

```text id="q53qtp"
Aurelia

↓

Rules

↓

Kingdom
```

is not the same as:

```text id="6mywfr"
Kingdom

↓

Rules

↓

Aurelia
```

Direction is part of the relationship definition.

---

# Symmetric Relationships

Some relationships naturally work both ways.

Examples:

```text id="cydbhu"
Married To

Sibling Of

Allied With
```

The Link Profile can declare whether a relationship is:

- Directional
- Symmetric
- Reciprocal

This allows the engine to behave correctly without hardcoding special cases.

---

# Relationship Profiles

Just as Nodes use Profiles, Relationships use Link Profiles.

Example:

```text id="tvxtfj"
Employment

Fields

Position

Department

Start Date

End Date

Notes
```

Another example:

```text id="9qgw9c"
Family

Fields

Relationship Strength

Legal Status

Birth Order

Notes
```

Different kinds of relationships can carry different metadata while sharing the same underlying engine.

---

# Link Ownership

Links are project-level entities.

They are not owned by either connected Node.

Instead:

```text id="tejlwm"
Project

↓

Link

↓

Source

↓

Target
```

This prevents accidental deletion when a Node is temporarily archived and keeps the relationship model consistent.

---

# Link Metadata

Each Link stores lightweight metadata.

```text id="qk8m76"
Relationship Type

Created Date

Modified Date

Visibility

Profile

Tags

Description (optional)
```

Metadata is separate from the relationship's semantic meaning.

---

# Offline Guarantee

All Link functionality operates without internet access.

Creating, editing, validating, searching, and navigating Links must work entirely on local project data.

---

# Acceptance Criteria

Version 1 Link Foundation is complete when:

- Every Link has a UUID.
- Every Link connects exactly two Nodes.
- Relationship Types are required.
- Direction is supported.
- Symmetric relationships are supported.
- Link Profiles are defined.
- Offline operation is guaranteed.

---

# One idea I think would make Links even stronger

While writing this, I noticed something we haven't explicitly designed yet:

## Relationship Confidence

Not every fact in a fictional world is equally certain.

For example:

```text id="9gtl4r"
Aurelia

↓

Possibly Descended From

↓

Ancient Kings
```

That isn't the same as:

```text id="n8gxch"
Aurelia

↓

Daughter Of

↓

King Roland
```

So I think Links should optionally include a **Confidence** field.

Examples:

- Confirmed
- Probable
- Rumored
- Unknown
- Disputed

This would be especially valuable for mystery novels, detective stories, historical fiction, RPG campaigns, and collaborative lore where not every relationship is an established fact.

Importantly, it stays **optional**, so it doesn't complicate ordinary projects but provides extra expressive power when needed.

---

```text id="xv2gqe"
███████░░░░░░░░░░░░░

Part 1 ✅ Foundation

Part 2 ⏳ Relationship Types

Part 3 ⏳ Metadata

Part 6 ⏳ Performance

Part 7 ⏳ Engine Contract
```

## Before Part 2

One design choice I'd like us to make is this:

Instead of shipping LoreCanvas with hundreds of built-in relationship types, I think Version 1 should include a **small, carefully curated library** of common relationship types (family, location, ownership, organization, chronology, etc.), while allowing users to create their own.

That keeps the software approachable for new users while giving experienced writers the flexibility to model unique worlds without waiting for updates. I think that balance matches the overall philosophy we've followed throughout the project: **strong defaults with room to grow.**

# LC-LINK-001
# Part 2 – Relationship Types & Profiles

## Philosophy

> **Relationships should be meaningful, extensible, and understandable.**

A relationship type defines **what a connection means**, while a relationship profile defines **what information that connection carries**.

---

# 1. Relationship Library

LoreCanvas includes a curated set of built-in relationship types.

### Family

```text id="lkr2xa"
Parent Of

Child Of

Sibling Of

Married To

Guardian Of
```

---

### Organization

```text id="mqc3pt"
Member Of

Leader Of

Works For

Reports To

Owns
```

---

### Geography

```text id="u38v2j"
Lives In

Located In

Borders

Originates From

Travels To
```

---

### Story

```text id="v1e4nf"
Mentor Of

Enemy Of

Friend Of

Companion Of

Rival Of
```

---

### Worldbuilding

```text id="y7azgf"
Created

Uses

Contains

Controls

Protects
```

These serve as sensible defaults, not limitations.

---

# 2. Custom Relationship Types

Users can create their own relationship types.

Example:

```text id="6ms5ks"
Bonded Through Magic

Competes In

Inherited Title From

Commands Fleet

Keeper Of
```

Each custom type behaves exactly like a built-in one.

---

# 3. Relationship Profiles

Each relationship type is assigned a profile that defines its available fields.

Example:

```text id="z3xtjr"
Employment Profile

Fields

Position

Department

Start Date

End Date

Notes
```

Another example:

```text id="9w9gq2"
Family Profile

Fields

Birth Order

Adopted

Legal Status

Notes
```

Profiles make relationships flexible without requiring different engines.

---

# 4. Direction Rules

Each relationship declares its behavior.

### Directional

```text id="h0wln6"
Employs

↓

Works For
```

---

### Symmetric

```text id="tbj5u0"
Married To

Sibling Of

Allied With
```

Both Nodes share the same relationship.

---

### Reciprocal

```text id="0s6x1m"
Mentor Of

↓

Student Of
```

The system can automatically expose the reciprocal view while storing one underlying relationship.

---

# 5. Categories

Relationship types belong to categories.

```text id="8b6fmd"
Family

Organization

Location

Story

Magic

Political

Military

Technology

Custom
```

Categories improve filtering, searching, and graph visualization.

---

# 6. Display Rules

Every relationship type may define:

- Display name
- Optional icon
- Color hint (presentation only)
- Short description

Presentation settings remain separate from relationship logic.

---

# 7. Default Metadata

Relationship profiles may define default values.

Example:

```text id="gjq2rh"
Employment

Department

Unknown

Start Date

Not Specified
```

Defaults reduce repetitive data entry while remaining editable.

---

# 8. Validation Rules

Profiles may enforce simple validation.

Examples:

- Required fields.
- Date format.
- Numeric ranges.
- Text length.

Complex validation can be added in future versions without changing the engine.

---

# 9. Offline Guarantee

Creating, editing, and managing relationship types and profiles works entirely offline.

No cloud services are required.

---

# 10. Acceptance Criteria

Version 1 is complete when:

- Built-in relationship library exists.
- Custom relationship types are supported.
- Relationship profiles are implemented.
- Direction rules are defined.
- Categories are available.
- Display rules are configurable.
- Basic validation exists.
- Offline operation is guaranteed.

---

# A new idea while writing this

I think we should introduce **Relationship Templates**.

They're different from Relationship Types.

For example:

## Relationship Type

```text id="w1o6np"
Mentor Of
```

defines **what** the relationship is.

A **Relationship Template** provides a ready-to-use starting point.

Example:

```text id="clw5gd"
Master and Apprentice

Relationship Type

Mentor Of

Default Metadata

Duration: Unknown

Status: Active

Training Style: Traditional
```

Or:

```text id="n4hdje"
Royal Marriage

Relationship Type

Married To

Default Metadata

Political Alliance: Yes

Heir Produced: No

Ceremony Date: Unknown
```

Templates speed up repetitive worldbuilding without locking users into fixed structures.

## One architectural refinement

While writing Part 2, I noticed a pattern we've repeated across the project:

- **Node Templates** initialize Nodes.
- **Card Templates** initialize Cards.
- **Relationship Templates** initialize Links.

Rather than treating these as separate systems, I think LoreCanvas should eventually have a **unified Template Engine** that all three use. Each template would simply target a different object type.

That keeps the implementation consistent and reduces duplicate code, while preserving the flexibility we've designed into each engine.

I think that's a cleaner architecture than having three independent template systems, and it fits naturally with everything we've built so far.

## I also have one refinement that fits your suggestion.

Instead of giving every engine its own separate import/export logic, I'd create a dedicated **Import/Export Engine** later in the project.

Its job would be to coordinate all imports and exports.

For Version 1, it would support just these operations:

```text

• Package
• Template

Export

• Project
• Package
• Template
```

Everything else, Nodes, Cards, Links, Assets, Profiles, and Templates, is bundled inside those containers as needed.

That keeps the interface extremely short while still giving us a robust architecture underneath.

I actually think this is cleaner than having each engine expose its own import/export functionality. Each engine simply knows how to serialize and deserialize its own data, while the Import/Export Engine orchestrates the process. It follows the same "one engine, one responsibility" rule we've been applying throughout LoreCanvas, and it keeps the user's workflow pleasantly simple.


Each engine already knows how to save and load its own data.

```text
↓
```

Suppose in Version 3 we add:

- AI Memory Engine
- Plugin Engine
- Collaboration Engine

The Import/Export Engine simply asks every registered engine:

If yes, it includes that data.

If not, it moves on.

That's a clean extension point that doesn't disturb the rest of the architecture.

# I think we should add one architectural rule

I'd write it like this:

> **Every engine is responsible for serializing and validating its own data. The Import/Export Engine is responsible only for orchestrating the exchange of data between engines and external files.**

That sentence clearly separates responsibilities:

- The **Node Engine** knows how to represent Nodes.
- The **Card Engine** knows how to represent Cards.
- The **Link Engine** knows how to represent Links.
- The **Import/Export Engine** never needs to understand the internal structure of those objects. It simply coordinates the process.

That means all the work we've already done on the Node Engine and Card Engine remains valid. We aren't rewriting their responsibilities, we're just giving them a single coordinator to work with.

I actually think this makes the architecture stronger than our earlier design because it keeps import/export concerns in one dedicated place while preserving the modularity we've been aiming for since the beginning.

# LC-IO-001
# Import / Export Engine

## Engineering Philosophy

> **Moving projects should be as effortless as opening a folder.**

The Import/Export Engine coordinates the transfer of data while allowing every engine to remain responsible for its own information.

It never owns project data.

It only moves it safely.

---

# Responsibilities

The Import/Export Engine is responsible for:

- Import orchestration
- Export orchestration
- Package creation
- Package extraction
- Compatibility verification
- Integrity verification
- Progress reporting
- Error reporting

It is **not** responsible for understanding Nodes, Cards, or Links.

---

# What It Does NOT Own

The engine never stores or edits:

- Nodes
- Cards
- Links
- Profiles
- Templates
- Assets
- Settings

Those remain the responsibility of their respective engines.

---

# User Operations

Version 1 intentionally keeps the interface small.

## Import

```text id="9xnk3e"
Import Project

Import Package

Import Template
```

---

## Export

```text id="g8ucit"
Export Project

Export Package

Export Template
```

That's the complete public interface.

---

# Internal Workflow

When exporting:

```text id="sk0klc"
User

↓

Export Project

↓

Import/Export Engine

↓

Repository Engine

↓

Node Engine

↓

Card Engine

↓

Link Engine

↓

Profile Engine

↓

Template Engine

↓

Package Builder

↓

.lore package
```

The same flow works in reverse during import.

---

# Project Export

A Project Export contains everything needed to reopen the project.

Example:

```text id="h6mjq0"
Project

↓

Nodes

Cards

Links

Profiles

Templates

Assets

Settings

Snapshots

Manifest
```

The user receives a single portable package.

---

# Package Export

Packages are smaller.

A package may contain:

```text id="2n9dqi"
Selected Nodes

↓

Required Cards

↓

Relationships

↓

Assets

↓

Dependencies
```

The exporter automatically gathers required dependencies.

For example:

Exporting a Kingdom automatically includes:

- Kingdom Node
- Kingdom Cards
- Flag Image
- Timeline
- Connected Leaders (optional)
- Relationship definitions

No manual selection is required.

---

# Template Export

Templates are completely independent.

Example:

```text id="p3vhsw"
Fantasy Character Template

↓

Profile

↓

Default Cards

↓

Default Properties

↓

Preview Image
```

These can be shared without exposing an entire project.

---

# Package Manifest

Every exported file contains a small manifest.

Example:

```text id="euv8gn"
LoreCanvas Version

Package Version

Created Date

Project Name

Required Features

Package Type

Checksum
```

This allows compatibility checks before import.

---

# Compatibility

Before importing:

```text id="sn5kg4"
Read Manifest

↓

Check Version

↓

Check Required Features

↓

Verify Integrity

↓

Import
```

If something isn't compatible, the user gets a clear explanation before any changes are made.

---

# Integrity Verification

Every package includes a checksum.

On import:

- Verify checksum.
- Verify structure.
- Verify required files.
- Verify references.

Only then does the import begin.

---

# Failure Behaviour

If an import fails:

- No partial project is created.
- Existing projects remain untouched.
- Temporary files are cleaned up.
- A clear error report is generated.

Imports behave as transactions.

---

# Offline Guarantee

Importing and exporting work entirely offline.

No online activation, account verification, or cloud storage is required.

---

# Acceptance Criteria

Version 1 is complete when:

- Project import/export works.
- Package import/export works.
- Template import/export works.
- Compatibility is verified.
- Integrity is verified.
- Imports are transactional.
- Offline operation is guaranteed.

---

# One improvement I'd like to add

I think LoreCanvas should use **one primary package format** instead of many.

For example:

```text id="k3afqz"
.lore
```

Inside that package, the engine stores whatever is needed:

```text id="hhm6hy"
manifest.json

nodes/

cards/

links/

profiles/

templates/

assets/

settings/
```

The user only ever sees **one file type**.

Whether it's a Project, Package, or Template is determined by the manifest.

That means:

- Double-clicking a `.lore` file always opens LoreCanvas.
- Drag-and-drop always works the same way.
- Future versions can extend the format without introducing new file extensions.

---

## 📊 Updated Architecture

```text id="v7c2lu"
Foundation                ✅
Architecture              ✅
Database                  ✅

Node Engine               ✅
Card Engine               ✅

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

Import/Export Engine      ✅ (Architecture)

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

Link Engine               ⏳
Query Engine              ⏳
Workspace Engine          ⏳
Repository Engine         ⏳
UI Engine                 ⏳
Module Engine             ⏳
```

## One refinement for implementation

I'd make the `.lore` package **zip-compatible** internally.

That doesn't mean users need to know it's a ZIP archive, but it gives us several advantages:

- Mature, well-tested compression.
- Faster implementation.
- Easy debugging during development.
- Better portability across operating systems.

LoreCanvas would treat `.lore` as its own package format, while internally using a standard compressed archive containing the manifest and structured project data.

That gives us a professional-looking format without reinventing archive technology, and it stays perfectly aligned with the modular architecture we've been building.

## Rule 4

Never through shortcuts.

# Where I think we go next

Now that we've completed:

- ✅ Node Engine
- ✅ Card Engine
- ✅ Import/Export architecture

I think the **Repository Engine** should actually come **before** we continue the Link Engine.

Why?

Because every engine we've designed already assumes that a Repository exists.

Right now we've described *what* Nodes, Cards, and Links are.

The Repository Engine defines *where* they live, *how* they're stored, *how* they're loaded, and *how* every other engine interacts with them.

In software architecture terms, it's the central librarian. It doesn't decide what a book contains, but it always knows where to find it, how to catalog it, and how to hand it to the right person.

By defining it now, the Link Engine, Query Engine, and Workspace Engine will all have a solid storage abstraction to build upon instead of making their own assumptions.

I actually think this is a cleaner order than our original roadmap, because it avoids revisiting storage decisions later. The foundation becomes:

1. **Database** (the physical data model)
2. **Repository Engine** (the storage and access layer)
3. **Node Engine** (concepts)
4. **Card Engine** (content)
5. **Link Engine** (relationships)
6. **Query Engine** (finding information)
7. **Workspace Engine** (the user's working environment)

Looking back, I think this revised sequence is more coherent and will make implementation in Replit significantly smoother because each layer builds directly on the one below it rather than skipping ahead and filling in gaps later.

# LC-REPO-001
# Repository Engine
## Part 1 – Foundation

---

# Engineering Philosophy

> **The Repository is the single source of truth for all project data.**

Every engine reads and writes through the Repository.

No engine accesses the database directly.

That one rule prevents an enormous number of bugs.

---

# The Repository's Role

Think of it as the project's librarian.

It doesn't decide what a Node is.

It doesn't edit Cards.

It doesn't validate Links.

Instead, it knows:

- where everything is,
- how to retrieve it,
- and how to save it safely.

---

# Architecture

```text
                Workspace

                    │

                    ▼

             Query Engine

                    │

                    ▼

             Card Engine

                    │

                    ▼

             Link Engine

                    │

                    ▼

             Node Engine

                    │

                    ▼

          Repository Engine

                    │

                    ▼

             Local Database
```

Every request eventually reaches the Repository.

---

# Responsibilities

The Repository Engine owns:

- Object storage
- Object retrieval
- Object registration
- Object lookup
- Transactions
- Asset references
- Project manifests
- Repository integrity

It **does not** own business logic.

---

# Repository Objects

Everything inside a project becomes a Repository Object.

Examples:

```text
Node

Card

Link

Profile

Template

Asset

Snapshot

Workspace Layout

Settings
```

Every object receives a Repository Entry.

---

# Repository Entry

Each stored object has standardized metadata.

```text
Repository ID

Object UUID

Object Type

Storage Location

Created Date

Modified Date

Checksum

Status
```

This metadata is managed automatically.

---

# Object Registration

Whenever an engine creates something:

```text
Node Engine

↓

Create Node

↓

Repository

↓

Register Object

↓

Return UUID
```

The Repository guarantees uniqueness.

---

# Object Lookup

Instead of asking:

> "Where is this file?"

Every engine asks:

```text
Repository

↓

Get(UUID)
```

The Repository handles the rest.

This keeps every engine independent of file locations.

---

# Transactions

Every write operation is transactional.

```text
Begin Transaction

↓

Write Objects

↓

Validate

↓

Commit

or

Rollback
```

No engine should ever leave the project in a partially updated state.

---

# Object States

Repository objects may be:

```text
Active

Archived

Deleted

Recoverable
```

The Repository tracks these consistently across all object types.

---

# Asset References

Large files such as images are stored separately.

Cards and other objects keep only references.

```text
Card

↓

Asset UUID

↓

Repository

↓

Image File
```

This avoids duplication and simplifies backups.

---

# Offline Guarantee

The Repository never depends on:

- Internet access
- Cloud storage
- User accounts
- Remote validation

Everything required for a project exists locally.

---

# Acceptance Criteria

The Repository Foundation is complete when:

- Every object is registered.
- Every object has standardized metadata.
- Transactions are supported.
- UUID lookup is implemented.
- Asset references are managed.
- Offline operation is guaranteed.

---

# One improvement I think we should adopt immediately

While writing this, I noticed an opportunity to make the Repository even cleaner.

Instead of storing objects in folders named after their types, the Repository should store them using a predictable internal structure while letting the engines decide how to interpret them.

Conceptually:

```text
Repository
│
├── Objects
├── Assets
├── Snapshots
├── Templates
├── Manifest
└── Indexes
```

The Repository doesn't care whether an object is a Node or a Card. It only knows that it's an object with a UUID and metadata.

The Node Engine interprets Node objects.

The Card Engine interprets Card objects.

The Link Engine interprets Link objects.

That keeps the Repository wonderfully generic.

---

I'd like to introduce one small but powerful rule:

> **The Repository should never know *why* an object exists, only *how* to store and retrieve it.**

That keeps the Repository completely reusable. If, years from now, LoreCanvas adds new object types such as AI memories, simulation states, or plugin data, the Repository won't need to change. It will simply store new objects using the same registration and transaction mechanisms we've already defined.

I think that's one of the strongest indicators of a long-lived architecture: the lowest layers remain stable even as the application above them evolves.

# LC-REPO-001
# Part 2 – Storage Model

---

# Engineering Philosophy

> **The storage model should remain stable even if the application grows for decades.**

In other words:

Features evolve.

Storage should barely change.

---

# Repository Layout

I think we should separate the repository into logical sections rather than by engine.

```text
.lore
│
├── manifest.json
│
├── objects/
│
├── assets/
│
├── templates/
│
├── snapshots/
│
├── indexes/
│
├── cache/
│
└── logs/
```

Each directory has exactly one purpose.

Nothing overlaps.

---

# Why not...

Instead of this:

```text
nodes/

cards/

links/
```

I recommend:

```text
objects/
```

Because the Repository shouldn't care what an object is.

It simply stores objects.

---

# Objects

Every Repository Object follows exactly the same outer structure.

```text
Object

↓

Header

↓

Metadata

↓

Payload
```

---

## Object Header

Every object begins with:

```text
UUID

Object Type

Version

Status
```

Nothing else.

---

## Metadata

Next comes:

```text
Created

Modified

Checksum

Repository Version

Tags

Flags
```

Again...

Exactly the same for every object.

---

## Payload

Only here does the Repository stop caring.

For example:

```text
Node Payload
```

or

```text
Card Payload
```

or

```text
Link Payload
```

The Repository simply stores the payload.

Only the owning engine understands it.

---

# Object Independence

Every object is completely independent.

Instead of embedding large structures:

```text
Character

↓

Biography

↓

Images

↓

Timeline
```

Store:

```text
Character UUID

↓

Card UUID

↓

Image UUID

↓

Timeline UUID
```

Everything references everything else.

Nothing duplicates.

---

# Assets

Assets live outside Objects.

```text
Assets

↓

UUID

↓

Image File
```

Cards never contain images.

They only reference Asset UUIDs.

---

# Templates

Templates receive the same treatment.

```text
Template UUID

↓

Metadata

↓

Payload
```

The Repository doesn't need to know whether it's:

- Character Template
- Kingdom Template
- Relationship Template

It simply stores another object.

---

# Snapshots

Snapshots are stored separately.

```text
Snapshots

↓

Snapshot UUID

↓

Object UUID

↓

Changes
```

Snapshots never replace Objects.

They only describe previous states.

---

# Indexes

Indexes exist purely for speed.

Examples:

```text
UUID Index

Name Index

Tag Index

Relationship Index
```

If an index becomes corrupted...

The Repository simply rebuilds it.

Indexes are never considered the source of truth.

---

# Cache

Cache is temporary.

Examples:

```text
Thumbnails

Search Cache

Recent Objects

Session Cache
```

The Repository may delete cache at any time.

Nothing important lives here.

---

# Logs

Logs help diagnose problems.

Examples:

```text
Recovery Log

Import Log

Export Log

Repository Log
```

Logs are optional but extremely useful during development and troubleshooting.

---

# Object References

All cross-object references use UUIDs.

Never file paths.

Never names.

Never positions.

This guarantees stability during:

- Renaming
- Reorganization
- Moving folders
- Localization

---

# Storage Principles

Every Repository Object obeys:

- One UUID.
- One owner.
- One payload.
- Immutable identity.
- Stable references.
- Independent storage.

These become universal rules across LoreCanvas.

---

# Acceptance Criteria

Storage Model is complete when:

- Repository layout is defined.
- Universal object format exists.
- Payload separation is documented.
- Asset storage is externalized.
- Snapshots are isolated.
- Indexes are rebuildable.
- Cache is disposable.
- UUID references are universal.

---

# One architectural improvement I think we should make

While writing this, I realized there's one more abstraction that will make the Repository even cleaner.

Instead of engines writing files directly, every write should go through a **Storage Adapter**.

Conceptually:

```text
Node Engine
        │
Card Engine
        │
Link Engine
        ▼
 Repository Engine
        ▼
 Storage Adapter
        ▼
 File System
```

In Version 1, the Storage Adapter simply writes to the local file system.

But in the future, we could add:

- Cloud storage adapters
- Encrypted storage adapters
- Read-only archive adapters
- Git-backed adapters
- Database-backed adapters

without changing the Repository Engine itself.

This keeps our architecture remarkably flexible while keeping Version 1 simple, because we only implement one adapter initially.

## One suggestion for implementation

I think we've reached the point where we should start classifying every architectural decision into one of three levels:

- **Core (Must Have):** Required for LoreCanvas to function correctly. Example: UUIDs, transactions, Repository layout.
- **Recommended:** Improves usability or maintainability but isn't essential for the first release. Example: rebuildable indexes, diagnostic logs.
- **Future Extension:** Reserved for later versions without affecting the core architecture. Example: cloud storage adapters, Git integration, encrypted repositories.

If we annotate our design documents this way, Replit (or any future developer) will know exactly what to implement first and what can safely be deferred, making the development process much smoother without compromising the overall vision.

# LC-REPO-001
# Part 3 – Transactions & Data Integrity

---

# Engineering Philosophy

> **A project should never exist in a half-saved state.**

Every change either completes successfully or leaves the project exactly as it was before.

---

# What is a Transaction?

A transaction is a controlled sequence of operations treated as one unit.

For example:

```text id="y9x8p2"
Rename Character

↓

Update Node

↓

Update Biography Card

↓

Update References

↓

Update Search Index

↓

Commit
```

If one step fails:

```text id="3r2kz1"
Rename Character

↓

Update Node

↓

Update Biography Card

↓

ERROR

↓

Rollback
```

Everything returns to the previous state.

No partial changes remain.

---

# Transaction Lifecycle

Every transaction follows the same lifecycle.

```text id="8f4djm"
Start

↓

Validate

↓

Execute

↓

Verify

↓

Commit

or

Rollback
```

This lifecycle is shared across the application.

---

# Transaction Scope

Transactions may involve:

- One object
- Multiple objects
- Entire project operations

Examples:

### Small

```text id="c7s4la"
Edit Card
```

### Medium

```text id="m5q8fw"
Rename Character

↓

Update Links

↓

Update References
```

### Large

```text id="k2v9ne"
Import Project
```

The Repository handles them using the same transaction model.

---

# Validation Phase

Before any data is written:

The Repository checks:

- Object exists
- UUID is valid
- References are valid
- Required assets exist
- Storage is available
- No conflicting locks

If validation fails, nothing is written.

---

# Staging Area

I think every transaction should use a temporary staging area.

```text id="n8h5yv"
Repository

↓

Staging

↓

Validation

↓

Commit
```

Only after validation succeeds are the changes merged into the Repository.

This greatly reduces the risk of corruption.

---

# Atomic Commit

A commit is all-or-nothing.

```text id="7u4mjk"
Success

↓

All changes become visible
```

or

```text id="g9e2qx"
Failure

↓

No changes become visible
```

Users never see an incomplete operation.

---

# Rollback

If a transaction cannot finish:

```text id="6v1rtb"
Discard Staging

↓

Restore Previous State

↓

Report Error
```

Rollback must leave the Repository exactly as it was before the transaction began.

---

# Transaction Log

Every completed transaction creates a lightweight log entry.

Example:

```text id="b4q7sz"
Transaction ID

Timestamp

Operation

Objects Affected

Result

Duration
```

These logs support debugging and recovery without storing sensitive project content.

---

# Nested Transactions

For Version 1, I recommend we **do not support nested transactions**.

One transaction runs at a time.

If another operation needs changes, it waits.

This keeps the implementation much simpler and reduces the chance of subtle bugs.

If future requirements justify it, nested transactions can be introduced later.

---

# Crash Recovery

If the application closes during a transaction:

```text id="w3k8pd"
Restart

↓

Detect Incomplete Transaction

↓

Discard Staging Area

↓

Restore Last Valid Repository
```

The Repository always opens in a valid state.

---

# Concurrency

Version 1 assumes a single active editor for a project.

That means:

- No simultaneous write conflicts.
- Simpler locking.
- Easier debugging.
- Better offline reliability.

If collaborative editing is added in the future, it will build on this foundation rather than replace it.

---

# Offline Guarantee

Transactions require no internet connection.

All validation, staging, commits, and recovery occur entirely on the local machine.

---

# Acceptance Criteria

Transactions are complete when:

- Every write uses a transaction.
- Validation occurs before writing.
- Staging is implemented.
- Commits are atomic.
- Rollback restores the previous state.
- Crash recovery restores a valid repository.
- Transaction logs are created.
- Offline operation is guaranteed.

---

# One improvement I think is worth adding

I'd introduce a **Transaction Coordinator** inside the Repository Engine.

Conceptually:

```text id="h2n7wf"
Node Engine
      │
Card Engine
      │
Link Engine
      │
Import Engine
      ▼
Transaction Coordinator
      ▼
Repository
```

Instead of every engine managing its own commits, they all ask the Transaction Coordinator to perform repository updates.

The coordinator then:

- Starts the transaction.
- Validates the request.
- Manages the staging area.
- Executes writes.
- Verifies integrity.
- Commits or rolls back.

This centralizes transaction logic in one place, ensuring every engine follows the same rules and making the entire system easier to maintain.

### One final refinement

I think we should add one more repository principle that complements everything we've built:

> **The Repository never guesses. It either commits verified data or commits nothing.**

That philosophy eliminates "best effort" saves, which are often the source of silent corruption. If something isn't safe to write, LoreCanvas should stop, explain the issue, and preserve the last known good state. For a writing platform where users may invest years into a single project, I think that level of reliability is well worth prioritizing.

# LC-REPO-001
# Part 4 – Asset Management

---

# Engineering Philosophy

> **Creative assets are first-class project resources, not attachments.**

An image, audio clip, PDF, or map isn't just a file sitting next to a project. It's a managed asset with its own identity and lifecycle.

---

# Why an Asset System?

Without one, projects quickly become messy:

```text id="a1m4zq"
chapter_final.png

chapter_final2.png

chapter_final_REAL.png

map_new.png

map_new_fixed.png
```

Instead, LoreCanvas treats every asset as a managed object.

---

# Asset Lifecycle

```text id="b2k8rd"
Import

↓

Register

↓

Reference

↓

Use

↓

Archive

↓

Delete
```

Every asset follows this lifecycle regardless of its type.

---

# Asset Identity

Every asset receives:

```text id="c3v9lf"
Asset UUID

Original Filename

Asset Type

Created Date

Modified Date

Checksum

Status
```

Cards and Links always reference the Asset UUID, never the file path.

---

# Supported Asset Types (Version 1)

To keep Version 1 focused:

### Images

- PNG
- JPG/JPEG
- WEBP
- GIF (static display)

---

### Documents

- PDF
- TXT
- Markdown

---

### Data

- CSV
- JSON (for imports/templates)

Future versions can add:

- Audio
- Video
- 3D models
- Fonts
- Custom asset types

---

# Asset Storage

Internally:

```text id="d4n2pw"
assets/

↓

UUID

↓

Stored File
```

The Repository decides where the physical file lives.

The rest of the application only knows the UUID.

---

# Asset References

Multiple objects can safely share one asset.

```text id="e5f8hn"
Map Image

↓

Asset UUID

↓

Kingdom Card

↓

World Card

↓

Timeline Event
```

Only one physical copy exists.

---

# Metadata

Each asset stores lightweight metadata.

Examples:

```text id="f6j3xm"
Display Name

Original Filename

Import Date

Size

Type

Tags

Description
```

For images, additional metadata may include:

- Width
- Height
- Thumbnail status

---

# Thumbnail Generation

For supported image types:

```text id="g7l5yb"
Import Image

↓

Generate Thumbnail

↓

Store Thumbnail

↓

Display Preview
```

Thumbnail generation runs in the background and never blocks the user.

---

# Asset Validation

Before registration:

- Verify file integrity.
- Verify supported type.
- Detect duplicates using checksum.
- Reject corrupted files.

This helps keep repositories clean.

---

# Duplicate Detection

If the same file is imported twice:

```text id="h8p6vc"
Compare Checksum

↓

Already Exists?

↓

Yes

↓

Reuse Existing Asset
```

The user can choose to:

- Reuse the existing asset.
- Import a separate copy if they intentionally want two independent assets.

---

# Asset Usage Tracking

The Repository maintains a reverse lookup.

```text id="i9r7wd"
Asset UUID

↓

Referenced By

Card A

Card B

Node C
```

Benefits:

- Safe deletion.
- "Where is this used?" view.
- Orphan detection.

---

# Orphan Assets

An asset with no references becomes an orphan.

The Repository can suggest cleanup:

```text id="j0s8xe"
Unused Assets

↓

Review

↓

Delete

or

Keep
```

Nothing is removed automatically.

---

# Asset Export

During Project or Package export:

The Import/Export Engine asks the Repository:

> "Which assets are required?"

Only referenced assets are included.

Unused assets stay behind unless the user explicitly chooses a full archive.

---

# Offline Guarantee

Every asset operation works locally:

- Import
- Preview
- Thumbnail generation
- Validation
- Usage tracking
- Cleanup
- Export

No cloud storage is required.

---

# Acceptance Criteria

Asset Management is complete when:

- Assets have UUIDs.
- Supported file types are defined.
- Duplicate detection exists.
- Metadata is stored.
- Thumbnail generation is available.
- Usage tracking is implemented.
- Orphan detection is available.
- Offline operation is guaranteed.

---

# One improvement I'd like to add

I think we should introduce the idea of an **Asset Collection**.

This is not a new asset type.

It's simply a logical grouping.

For example:

```text id="k1t9zf"
Character Artwork

↓

Portrait

Expression Sheet

Reference Sketches

Official Illustration
```

Or:

```text id="l2u0ag"
Kingdom Maps

↓

Political Map

Terrain Map

Trade Routes

Climate Map
```

Collections don't duplicate files. They just organize related assets, making large projects much easier to navigate.

## One architectural observation

As we've built the Repository Engine, a pattern has emerged:

- **Repository** manages storage.
- **Import/Export** moves data.
- **Node** manages concepts.
- **Card** manages content.
- **Link** manages relationships.

Each engine has a very clear responsibility and communicates through well-defined interfaces. That's exactly the modular architecture we were aiming for.

At this point, I wouldn't change that direction. Instead, I'd continue reinforcing it in the remaining Repository sections so that when we eventually start implementing LoreCanvas in Replit, each engine can be developed and tested independently before being integrated into the whole system.
